In this study, researchers examined the behavior of largest losses or gains in financial portfolios by analyzing random matrices and their statistical properties. Through this, they gained insights into how portfolio managers might mitigate severe outcomes and their results hold broader implications for understanding critical phenomena in complex systems.

Quantum entanglement between coupled cavities and external modes plays a crucial role in optical phenomena and offers opportunities to improve precision in phase measurements. A fundamental model involving two-mode bosonic systems is examined, where each cavity contains molecules with long-lived dipolar interactions, and the exchange of photons reflects optical phase fluctuations. By focusing on squeezing properties, we investigate entanglement and its relation to optical phase sensitivity. When the system is in a coherent state, both classical and quantum contributions to squeezing are analyzed in relation to optical phase fluctuations. Furthermore, in a two-photon state, only quantum effects are responsible for squeezing in this system. When the optical mode is in a mixed state due to random phase fluctuations, there is still a possibility of observing non-classical squeezing. The presence of dipoolelectric interactions enhances squeezing, and this phenomenon is crucial for observing non-classical properties in isolated systems. This model has real-world applications, such as in trapping ions in optical cavities, and can contribute to the development of advanced quantum sensing techniques.

A key challenge in constructing complete genomes using long-read sequencing data is breaking down the extremely long continuous reads produced into more manageable fragments. Although this 'contig production' process can be efficiently executed on a single CPU, it becomes a significant bottleneck when working with large datasets on a single machine, and is even more pronounced in a cluster environment where each node has fewer resources. In this research, we develop and implement an algorithm to break down these long reads into smaller fragments in a distributed computing environment, and test its performance on real-world genomic datasets. Our results show that this algorithm can effectively produce contigs in a distributed manner, and outperforms a cluster-based implementation by a factor of up to 3.4 times, with the performance gap increasing substantially as the size of the dataset grows. When compared to existing software tools, our implementation is found to produce the most accurate results with an error rate nearly 4 times lower than the next best tool.

A novel logistic equation, incorporating a delay factor, is developed from a cell biology model. 
The model's global dynamics are analyzed through an invariant positive equilibrium's assessment, 
then confirmed via phase plane and Borges-Machado Lyapunov functional analysis. 
The global stability of the equilibrium near the origin is established using a Lyapunov stability analysis, 
while the model's positive invariant region and unbounded solutions are demonstrated via a Lyapunov functional analysis. 
The model's global dynamics are summarized in a dichotomy result, offering insights into unbounded solution behavior.

The use of statistical depths has become a popular method for evaluating and comparing the efficiency of dry weight estimators, which can be applied to the analysis of compositional data, regardless of the dry weight procedure employed, provided the data is expressed as a percentage of a suitable reference. Some depth measures, however, are sensitive to the dry weight method, which can pose a problem during the comparison of different point estimation procedures. To address this issue, this paper proposes a new approach that involves incorporating the isometric log-ratio transformation into the depth measure, thereby ensuring its reliability, whatever dry weight method is used. To demonstrate the efficacy of this method, the proposed approach is employed in an analysis of the efficiency of several point estimation procedures for a data set consisting of microbial community measurements.

A particular setup consisting of a capton nanowire and an NbN nanowire connected in series, placed on a Si substrate with a SiO2 mask, has been found to exhibit stable, long-lasting electrical current, known as a Josephson effect. This phenomenon occurs when a significant electric current flows from one material to another through a thin layer, driven by the transfer of energy between the materials. This setup displays two key properties: first, the device shows an obvious current pattern with respect to bias voltage; second, the setup exhibits steady, long-lasting electrical current, known as a zero-bias resonance, which is a hallmark of the device exhibiting perfect electrical current transfer under certain conditions. This setup has been found to maintain stability in a wide range of temperatures and pressures. This discovery has potential applications in developing highly sensitive sensors capable of detecting tiny magnetic fields and highly sensitive detectors of tiny electric currents.

Researchers from the RIKEN Nishina Center for Accelerator-based Physics and the University of Tokyo performed a series of experiments using fragmentation of 58Fe ions on a CH2 target to study isomers in germanium isotopes around N = 40. Specifically, they focused on 57Ge, a 5/2+ isomer with a half-life of 20.7 days, located near a stable 57Ge state with a 9/2+ configuration. Experiments were carried out at the RIKEN Radioisotope Center using a Wilkinson-type magnetic spectrometer to measure mass, beta energy, and beta asymmetry. Data collection included 57Ge decays into 57K and 56K, as well as 56Ge decays into 56K and 56K. Through a comparison of experimental and theoretical beta-corrected yield curves, researchers determined that 57Ge's total decay strength is 2420(290) s-1 into 57K and 56K, a value significantly higher than previous estimates of 840(160) s-1. This discrepancy, along with previously measured total decay strengths for 58Ge and 59Ge, led researchers to conclude that 57Ge's decay strength increases steadily throughout the region around N = 40. Using a set of shell-model and multilevel unfolding calculations based on the GXD interaction, researchers proposed that 57Ge's ground state has a shaded-probability of

Researchers have introduced an innovative technique called isochronous mass spectrometry that enables the measurement of precise masses for short-lived nuclei at the COO I-200ME mass storage system. This method uses velocity-defined time-of-flight and magnetic rigidity-defined time-of-flight to identify isotopic sequences, which are then used to calculate masses. By analyzing the isotopic sequences of a large number of known nuclei, precise mass measurements can be obtained for unknown nuclei based on isobaric comparisons. This technique was tested by taking two ion beams from a tandem van de Graaff accelerator, one for a reference nucleus ($^{22}$Na) and the other for a short-lived nucleus near it. By comparing their isotopic sequences, the mass of the unknown nucleus can be calculated. This technique was demonstrated by obtaining a very precise mass for $^{58}$Mn, which is in agreement with the current experimental value and exhibits high precision.

The All-Hands Meeting 2021 for the LHC and lattice field theory communities combined in a virtual conference, addressing the gap between numerical simulations and theoretical models through their respective outcomes. This paper presents a method for converting simulation data into probability distributions that match theoretical predictions, specifically for quantum field theories. It discusses various challenges in standardizing simulation outcomes for multiple theoretical models.

This paper addresses the challenge of structured text recognition by analyzing a range of structured formats within real-world images, drawing from various datasets to train its model. Our research focuses on leveraging regular expressions as a guiding principle to favor accurate structural analysis, thus distinguishing our approach from existing work. Evaluations using the ICDAR 2013 Challenge dataset revealed that our method demonstrates consistent recognition accuracy across different structural formats, outperforming the state-of-the-art deep learning-based approaches. Furthermore, our technique proves adaptable to various structural formats and is highly efficient in terms of processing speed and memory requirements. To facilitate future research, we have developed an open-source platform and made our code available on GitHub, alongside a structural text recognition benchmarking framework. This platform enables users to easily create and fine-tune models for a range of structured text challenges.

The LHCb experiment has examined the creation of top and bottom quarks in proton-nucleus collisions at an energy of 13 TeV. Between 2015 and 2018, the experiment collected data on a dataset consisting of 36 pb^-1 of proton-lead and 3 pb^-1 of lead-proton collisions. The experiment detected the production of 33,736 top quark pairs and 40,322 bottom quark pairs. The study of various distribution shapes of these events confirms previous findings and provides new constraints on the production of a hypothetical fifth force for both top and bottom quarks. The study also placed the first constraint on the production of same-sign same-flavour top quark pairs in the Standard Model, with a predicted cross-section of 5.03 +0.44/-0.41 pb. The experiment also detected individual elements of these events: the beta decay of 9.3 million W bosons and 6.2 million D mesons, which were used to study the collision conditions and nucleon energy loss. The data was found to be consistent with the predicted rates of these events in the Standard Model. The study also provided new constraints on the production of long-lived particles that may interact in the detector, as well as the production of top quarks in the forward region of the experiment. The may have been detected by the experiment with a significance of 2.5 standard deviations. The analysis of the experiment may provide the first

This study focuses on key elements in developing a Text-to-SQL model that can effectively handle various forms of language interactions. It breaks down the analysis process into three crucial components: semantic frames, spatial relationships, and column references. Each component requires a deep understanding of the database schema and input text. Research has shown that individual column predictions are insufficient for analyzing semantic frames, but combining predictions from multiple columns provides better results. Additionally, accurate identification of spatial relationships depends on complete knowledge of row and column structures. To enhance Auxiliary Task performance, the team introduced a labeling mechanism for tree nodes, incorporating auxiliary labels to guide the model and facilitate learning. By incorporating this mechanism, the model achieved superior performance in identifying spatial relationships. However, column reference prediction remained a challenge. To address this problem, the team proposed a simple but effective routing network to substitute traditional fully connected layers in column reference models. This innovative network enabled the model to learn to ignore irrelevant columns and make more informed predictions based on the database schema alone. Experimental results demonstrated the model's superiority on the SpArt database dataset.

Radio astronomy has long depended on broad bandwidths for its benefits, but investigating bandwidth effects on radio source count and bias requires thorough investigation due to the limited data available. The initial findings from the Large Area Telescope and the LoTSS survey give us a chance to look into this, thanks to its broad bandwidth of 197 MHz and extensive coverage of the Northern sky. By utilizing noise simulations, we find that noise in flux measurements decreases slightly as the trial frequency increases within the observing bandwidth. This implies that flux bias varies with frequency, and due to the relationship between size and frequency, angular bias in radio sources also exists. This impact, however, may be masked by variability and further corrected by adjusting the spectral index. The findings from LoTSS SR also indicate that the distribution of radio source densities in the local universe follows a power-law, with inconsistencies in density maps likely resulting from residual ionospheric effects. The findings from this analysis support the idea that the growth of bias in radio sources is connected to their morphological characteristics.

A recently proposed model, the Ranking Bregman Branching Support Vector Machine, takes a versatile approach to address a challenging non-convex optimization problem. This issue arises in applications such as information retrieval and recommender systems, which involve large-scale datasets characterized by high-dimensional data types. To develop an efficient algorithm for solving this problem, we introduce a new adaptive-sampling technique and incorporate it into an existing branching search algorithm. This modification enhances the algorithm's sampling process by adapting to the characteristics of the data and significantly reducing the number of iterations required. As a result, our enhanced algorithm demonstrates substantially improved computational performance, particularly in high-dimensional scenarios, while maintaining accurate prediction accuracy.

Following a prior finding that entropy always increases in driven systems, it has been discovered that there are certain conditions under which the rate of entropy generation remains consistent or even declines. To explain this, a generalized version of the second law of thermodynamics was developed, which is applicable to systems undergoing rapid and gentle changes in state. It has been determined that, under these conditions, the rate at which entropy is produced does not vary and instead remains tied to the rate at which work is input into the system. This remains true regardless of the system's initial state, and even holds in the presence of multiple driving forces. To validate this theory, the prediction that entropy generation remains consistent was tested against a range of experimental and numerical data, including the movement of a particle in a potential landscape, the flow of a fluid through a series of expansions and compressions, and the simulation of a Brownian motor. In each of these cases, it was found that the rate of entropy generation remained consistent and could be accurately predicted using the newly developed entropy production rate formula. This has significant implications, as it suggests that there may be certain systems in which it is possible to achieve minimal or even zero entropy generation, despite the ongoing influence of driving forces.

Several AI-based environmental solutions have garnered attention for their potential to mitigate ecological problems, yet the full scope of their effects remains obscure. A case study investigation how companies promote green AI technologies in the US uncovers the current limitations in assessing these solutions. A common approach used to evaluate AI's environmental benefits is to measure its 'carbon footprint' impact, but this framework omits crucial considerations, such as the social connections of users and the solution's long-term ecological implications. As a result, the true ecological impact of many green AI technologies remains hidden from view, preventing comprehensive understanding and informed decision-making. To address this issue, we are developing a theoretical model to identify potential risks and benefits associated with AI-based environmental solutions, with a focus on their dynamic evolution over time. This theoretical model acknowledges that promoting green AI technologies can have negative social consequences, such as reinforcing existing environmental inequities, if they solely prioritize technical aspects without considering the diverse needs of vulnerable populations. To overcome this challenge, we are working to create an adaptive framework for identifying and addressing hidden ecological concerns related to AI-based environmental solutions.

Prescriptive Process Monitoring, a subcategory of Process Monitoring, relies on predictive processes known as prescriptive processes. These prescriptive processes aim to prevent issues at their root by implementing corrective actions before problems arise, thereby ensuring smooth business operations. To facilitate prescriptive monitoring, a comparative framework is required to assess various methods for identifying prescriptive processes. This paper introduces the PM\^2 index, a pioneering comparative framework, to help determine prescriptive processes through association rule mining techniques. Using this index, we evaluate eight different methods to establish a robust framework for prescriptive monitoring. The study also explores prescriptive process detection using association rule mining techniques, incorporating time constraints to enhance its effectiveness. To support our findings, we drawn from real-world examples in healthcare and hospitality industries. This extensive examination seeks to establish a standard for identifying prescriptive processes and paves the way for future improvements.

A region of interest is immersed in a heat transfer fluid with flows that influence the region's temperature and its property variation. The region's properties are described by a parameter $\chi$, and its value is sought after optimizing one or multiple desired goals. The optimal $\chi$ value can be found by solving a optimization problem tied to a weak formulation derived from the Boussinesq equation, and this will be the main focus of this research. A novel technique is proposed here to refine the optimization solution by improving its accuracy, and this involves controlling the size of the Boussinesq parameter $\epsilon$. The objective is to develop a method where the optimal $\chi$ solution can be obtained with minimal dependence on $\epsilon$, and this is achievable by maintaining a balance between the differences in velocity and temperature velocity increments and the difference in their directions. The proposed method is tested on a few challenging problems involving complex geometries, and the results show its effectiveness in regulating the optimization error with various $\epsilon$ values.

In algorithmic satisfiability theory, particular problems are examined which belong to the NP class and have fixed parameter independence. Specifically, we delve into "stacking problems" defined by a polynomial function, f, where each instance of the problem includes a set of elements, E, and a function, f, which assigns a value from the set {0,1}, to a subset of E, with a specified size, for a fixed, non-zero parameter, k. It's desirable to have these subsets, also referred to as "stacks," of size k, which exhibit a specific property, relative to a given set, with a specified property. We investigate various stacking problems by which we mean finding the smallest set, also referred to as "E", with a specified cardinality, which contains all possible "stacks", of size k, which exhibit a given property. One such problem, referred to as the "Nqueen's Problem in Knapsack" defines "E", as a subset of (N x N), which contains all "n" possible "k" sized stacks, which contain at most one "q", where 0 < or = "q", < "n". We investigate the "Nqueen's Problem in Knapsack" by showing its compact dependency on two parameters, "n" and "q", with a fixed parameter homomorphism, M, and derived classes, "Sat-And k-And" and "Sat-Or q-Or

Individuals may hold secret views that may diverge from their expressed opinions, especially when pressured by societal expectations. If given the opportunity, some people might reveal unconventional beliefs, such as supporting a minority political view, which could result in social ostracism or ridicule. A new model explores how people with pre-existing opinions, which might differ from their expressed beliefs, called "secrets," change over time. When secrets align with publicly expressed opinions, there's no change; however, when there's a discrepancy, external influences can shift both opinions and secrets. This external impact might stem from social interactions or exposure to facts. If external influences exceed a threshold, called "criticality," minor fluctuations can trigger sudden shifts in both secrets and opinions. As time progresses, opinions and secrets can rapidly switch many times as the system passes through various states of different stability levels. Eventually, the system settles into a stable equilibrium with fewer, but still possible, sudden shifts. When criticality is reached, even seemingly secure secrets can be exposed and the system, now aware of the discrepancy between opinions and secrets, settles into a new stable state with more frequent and repeated fluctuations. This research provides scientific backing for the notion that people adjust their views and secrets in response to external cues and uncovers structural properties of the system that allow for sudden changes.

A type of solution representing a black hole transition from subthermal to thermal equilibrium has been identified, characterized by an asymptotically flat spacetime and a "hairy" structure affecting radiation emission.

Understanding the temporal relationship between transcription and RNA synthesis is crucial, yet measuring RNA lag times remains challenging, especially in complex genomes. To address this, we've developed RAPID, a rigorous algorithm enabling the determination of RNA lag distributions for specific genes and broad chromosomal regions. Applying RAPID to Drosa phila cells using ChIP-qPCR and imaging data, we found a broad spectrum of RNA lag lengths, ranging from 30 minutes to over 100 minutes. Furthermore, RAPID identified variations in RNA lag among individual cells, correlated with differences in transcription duration, nascent RNA levels, and gene activity states. By analyzing the relationship between transcription characteristics and RNA lag, we discovered that long RNA lag genes are associated with increased transcription duration, distal locations, and PAF1 complex binding. Ultimately, RAPID provides a precise tool to investigate RNA synthesis delays across the entire genome, uncovering subtle differences among distinct chromosomal regions.

Researchers studying 64Ni with a zero-spin structure have discovered a unique state consisting of two components: a 0+ excited state at 2236.5 keV and a 2+ excited state at 2271.15 keV. By analyzing the 64Ni's nuclear matrix elements, it was found that these states exhibit distinct characteristics driven by different nuclear interactions. While a tensor interaction is responsible for excitation to the 2+ state, a monopole interaction is shown to be the primary driver for the 0+ state. Due to the monopole interaction's effect, the 64Ni's core transitions from a closed-shell to a core-excited state, showcasing the monopole interaction's significance in shaping nuclear structures.

Chiral gauge theories that lack supersymmetry are difficult to handle mathematically, but recent advances using 'delgating' have enabled us to overcome this challenge. As a direct result, new non-supersymmetric dualities have been discovered, offering fresh perspectives on chiral gauge theories. Additionally, these discoveries provide crucial insights into the broadest supersymmetric dualities, such as Seiberg duality. This concept has also been extended to incorporate fundamental matter, enabling us to analyze properties of related low-energy theories. Furthermore, these dualities can be applied to evaluate anomalies and representation weights in various chiral theories.

A linear complementary set of group codes is defined as a set of group codes where any two codes in the set have a linear intersection that equals the code's dimension. Our work focuses on constructing linear complementary sets of group codes over finite principal ideal rings and determining their properties. 

For a given ring, we established a construction method for linear complementary sets of group codes and proved that any set of group codes with a linear intersection of full depth can be part of such a set. Additionally, we discovered that linear complementary sets of group codes correspond to linear complementary sets of linear codes when the ring is a principal ideal ring. 

We also found that linear complementary sets of group codes over a certain ring have a 1-to-1 correspondence to linear supplementary sets of linear codes defined by a specific subset of the ring's elements. This relationship is particularly relevant in the context of polynomial rings, where linear complementary sets of group codes over such rings are constructed and their properties are examined. 

Furthermore, our work extends existing research on linear supplementary sets of group codes by applying the concept to group codes that do not have full rank. This generalization leads to a broader category of linear supplementary sets, and we construct several examples to illustrate this expansion.

Graphical models serve as a versatile framework for solving inference and optimization problems in discrete mathematics. Various algorithms have been developed to tackle these issues, with some leveraging belief propagation's efficiency within tractable regions. However, even simple algorithms using belief propagation can become performance-bottleneassistant

in larger datasets. On the other hand, more advanced methods like message passing and dual decomposition require more in-depth descriptions and computations, making them complex to implement and difficult to modify with optimizations. As a result, researchers and developers often avoid using these methods or creating new graphical model applications due to the complexity involved. 

We introduce a novel and efficient representation of a function that significantly reduces the complexity of using more advanced message passing and dual decomposition methods. This new representation enables simpler and more intuitive implementations, allowing for more adaptable and efficient modifications with optimizations. 

We use our proposed representation to provide the first dual decomposition algorithm for general factor graphs, alongside efficient message passing algorithms for inference and optimization tasks. The resulting algorithms outperform existing solutions in exact methods and provide a 2-3 order of magnitude performance improvement for certain numerical optimization problems on large datasets.

Human attention is drawn to a task by a combination of visual and auditory cues. These cues start to coordinate to capture attention, with the coordination timing varying depending on the situation. To study this coordination, a robot is programmed to participate in a basic task where it receives both visual and auditory signals indicating when an item has been dropped. The robot's goal is to determine when the dropped item becomes visible to both the visual and auditory senses. Research has demonstrated that robots equipped with advanced audio-visual capabilities can efficiently detect when the dropped item appears. This study has particularly highlighted the advantages of asynchronous coordination between audio and visual signals in this context.

Shear thickening transitions are rare events in viscoelastic fluids where their viscosity suddenly skyrockets. Previous research suggested that different materials respond to shear thickening in distinct, unique ways, much like fingerprints, and therefore, identifying the cause of a particular thickening mechanism is relatively easy. However, recent discoveries, including the creation of synthetic shear thickening materials, have revealed that various substances can exhibit similar patterns for different shear thickening transitions. This led to the hypothesis that there must be a universal pattern, common to all shear thickening transitions, and this pattern can help explain the causes of different mechanisms. Using advanced microviscosity models, researchers found that this universal pattern can reveal a wealth of information about the underlying microphysics of different materials. For example, it can determine whether a substance becomes more fluid-like or solid-like during a shear thickening event by analyzing the ratio of normal to shear stress. Furthermore, the pattern can provide information about the average duration of a shear thickening event, its rate of variation, and whether a substance responds to shear thickening in a sudden or gradual manner. By using this universal pattern, researchers can identify the microphysics of natural and artificial substances, and this can reveal interesting connections between various shear thickening materials, such as the similarity between the viscosity patterns of active matter and microgel suspensions.

Electrity, perceived as highly unpredictable, suffers from fluctuations in supply and demand, resulting in power crises due to an inability to match these variables. This study employs statistical modeling, combining real-world and simulated data, to explore electricity consumption patterns. The hour-of-the-day and day-of-the-week factors are used to model consumption, utilizing a binomial distribution for analysis. The study finds that electricity consumption exhibits predictable daily fluctuations but no discernible weekly patterns, driven primarily by hourly changes rather than diurnal rhythms.

The emphasis on data-driven methods and machine learning in scientific inquiry is profound. However, the reliance on external algorithms and pre-labeled training sets can introduce a degree of detachment, rendering researchers predominantly (and uncomfortably) dependent on external entities for data collection. This displacement of control may lead to a heightened risk of misinformation and biased inputs, similar to how Google's web search results may reflect personalized preferences. The interplay between technology and perception poses a significant, underappreciated threat to scientific integrity. This study investigates how Google's personalized search can result in the underdetection of relevant information and the overemphasis on irrelevant details. Using a randomized controlled trial methodology, we discovered that the lack of awareness about algorithmic biases in search engines can cause researchers to overlook crucial findings. Consequently, understanding and acknowledging the influences on our observations may lead to the development of proactive strategies to ensure transparency and accuracy in our research practices.

Automatically creating programs from detailed specifications is a task called program synthesis. A novel framework for generating code based on flow diagrams is presented, where a neural network is trained to predict program structures by analyzing visual elements of the diagrams. The framework employs Graph Identification Convolutional Neural Networks (GRCNN) to map cell regions to corresponding program structures, with the GRCNN framework consisting of multiple layers that process graphs representing program sections. Each GRCNN layer is trained to recognize distinct aspects of these graphs, with the framework being evaluated on a dataset of flow diagrams and their corresponding program structures. The synthesis of program structures from diagram cells is seen as a classification task, where each GRCNN layer is trained to predict a program structure from a given cell region. With each layer specializing in graph features at different levels, the framework is capable of accurately identifying and synthesizing program structures even from complex diagrams. The training data for the GRCNN framework is created by labeling regions of flow diagrams corresponding to program structures and their connections, with the framework being optimized through a backward propagation process in the training process. The framework's performance is evaluated using a metric that measures synthesis accuracy, where results show significant improvements over previous methods. A detailed analysis of the framework's results also shows that it can accurately predict low-level program structures even from poorly defined high-level diagrams, indicating its reliability and efficiency.

This analysis reveals that the widely-held expectation for low-dimensional modeling in climate science is unwarranted. Due to the interplay of several interacting climate systems, including atmospheric, oceanic, and terrestrial components with varied spatial extend, dimentionality in climate modeling is unlikely. 

We demonstrate that the core principles of dimensionality, including compactness and distinctiveness, are not met in climate systems. The complexity of interactions within individual systems, as well as between them, also violates these principles. 

Our research encompasses various diminution techniques, such as proper dimensionality reduction, that could facilitate meaningful low-dimensional representations of high-dimensional climate systems. Although diminution techniques can improve understanding and model efficiency, they do not address the core dimentionality issue. 

Our study also includes recent applications of diminution techniques in climate science and highlights the need for thorough assessments of these methods. Ultimately, diminution techniques are seen as temporary tools to aid climate research, with no attempt to establish a climatic low-dimensional framework.

The development of kilonova ejecta through the interaction of the r-process elements provides valuable insights into the nucleosynthesis occurring after a binary neutron star merger. To gain a deeper understanding, this process requires precise modeling that takes into account the atomic structures of the r-process elements. Recent advancements in relativistic atomic theory and high-level ab initio calculations have significantly improved the quality of atomic data, enabling the construction of level tables for essential low-energy states involved in the initial phases of kilonova ejecta. Building upon this, this research develops the atomic data needed for the Os isoelectronic sequence, specifically for Os I, Os II, Os III, Os IV, Hg-like Os, and Os-like Pt. Os I data are based on the Os I spectrum published by the NIST Atomic Spectra Database, while Os II, Os III, Os IV, Hg-like Os, and Os-like Pt data are created using the relativistic atomic structure code CIV3, which accounts for the Os IV 4s, 3s and 2s and the Hg-like Os 1s core. The newly calculated energy levels, oscillator strengths, and transition probabilities are used to create the first reliability tables for the Os isoelectronic sequence. These atomic data can now be incorporated into opacity codes to model the early stages of kilonova ejecta through the application of the relativistic bound-state model.

Our proposed study leverages deep learning and an ensemble of segmentation techniques to develop an automated gastrointestinal (GI) canal segmentation framework for a comprehensive clinical analysis. 

In the medical imaging domain, pulmonary vein segmentation is a particularly challenging task, and the difficulty is compounded when dealing with irregular heart rates, breathing patterns, and varying contrast agent dissemination. 

The development of accurate automatic segmentation software for the left atrium and pulmonary veins from computed tomography angiography (CTA) is crucial for enhanced clinical efficiency and robustness across different conditions. 

Our proposed dataset, comprised of 540 CTA images from 270 distinct patients, encompasses both healthy individuals and those with atrial fibrillation. 

We employed a two-stage process that combines convolutional neural networks (CNN) and iterative active contour models to fine-tune the segmentation. 

Our primary challenge lies in achieving accurate segmentation across the entire cardiac cycle, and we addressed this by adopting a fully convolutional CNN architecture designed for stable point-wise 3D image segmentation. 

The efficacy of our method was validated through comparison with commercial and open-source manual segmentation techniques on our comprehensive dataset. 

We observed significant improvements in segmentation precision using our automated approach, and the code has been successfully integrated into the clinical software environment. 

Additionally, our automated segmentation method has been successfully applied to achieve a high-resolution temporal resolution of 10 Hz for precise GI canal segmentation during CTA images. 

We compared the accuracy of our fully convolutional CNN-based approach with other traditional techniques

In various scientific and engineering disciplines, researchers encounter multi-dimensional data sets that can be represented as matrices. These data sets are often accompanied by relevant statistical or modeling problems, which require the implementation of linear algebra procedures. The compositional method offers a useful framework for data analysis, providing insights into data structure and relevance. However, the method's effectiveness heavily depends on the quality of linear algebra tools utilized to compute its components. The objective of this work is to contribute high-performance linear algebra technologies to the compositional method, facilitating its wide adoption among scientists and engineers. The article introduces a step-by-step guide to constructing and interpreting compositional figures, which reveal information about the dimensionality of data, its distribution, and the results of compositional analysis. The guide also covers various linear algebra procedures employed in its creation and interpretation. The authors present and discuss practical examples from different fields, which demonstrate the utility of compositional figures in revealing both noisy and significant data components.

Past research suggested that sub-Saturn mass exoplanets with low orbital radii were unlikely to have host stars with cool stellar properties, based on theoretical models. However, these past predictions conflicted with observational data from the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity survey, which indicated that about 15% of sub-Saturn mass exoplanets with low orbital radii are hosted by stars with low surface temperatures. To resolve this discrepancy, we used machine learning algorithms to create new theoretical models of sub-Saturn exoplanets with low orbital radii, which we then compared with observational data from the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity survey. These new models revealed that about 80% of sub-Saturn mass exoplanets with low orbital radii are hosted by stars with low surface temperatures, and that the remaining 20% are likely a mixture of planets with unusual properties and false positives. Our study also finds that most sub-Saturn mass exoplanets with low orbital radii are likely hosted by stars with a high fraction of heavy elements, which are necessary to form such planets. These findings suggest that most sub-Saturn mass exoplanets with low orbital radii are likely formed in environments with metal enrichment similar to that of our solar system.

To address the issue of distributing attention evenly among multiple domains, we develop a multi-domain attention network (MDAN), which simultaneously trains on multiple datasets. However, current multi-task learning methods often suffer from attention imbalance, causing some tasks to be overlooked by the model. To counter this, we propose a new algorithm called Tough Attention Regulation by Shared information maximization (TARS), which regulates the attention mechanism to equalize its treatment of each domain. TARS achieves this through two main components: first, it leverages the shared information among domains to enhance their distinct features; second, it uses a balance regulator (BR) to adjust the attention weights, ensuring they are closely aligned with the shared information. As a result, the model is forced to distribute attention fairly among domains. Our experimental validation, conducted across various public benchmarks and datasets, demonstrates the superior performance of TARS when compared to conventional attention mechanisms.

The compressed mass spectrum in the dark matter sector, a characteristic of certain models including the Wess-Zumino model and its extensions, is a logical outcome of a global symmetry being approximately $baryon-number-conserving$ in such theories. Dark matter comprising a single field is not feasible as it violates continuity, hence, we consider a doublet field to achieve this compressed mass spectrum. Introducing a Yukawa interaction with a confining gauge boson leads to binding forces that counteract mass compression. However, an unsuitable choice of interaction strengths results in fragmentation, contradicting the compressed mass hypothesis. Nevertheless, this model offers a distinct compressed mass scenario, a dark matter triplet, or a doublet with completely degenerate mass levels. Additionally, we examine the potential for detection of the dark matter by searching for residual heat within Earth's core or as a result of sunlight reflection off Earth's surface in the search for direct detection of the dark matter.

Inspired by the simplicity of reflex arcs in animal nervous systems, our neurobiologically-friendly model employs sparsely-interconnected neurons.
We successfully applied this model to a variety of learning tasks, achieving faster training times and improved generalization performance.
Our model's results outperformed previous research on numerous cognitive tasks, including navigation, object manipulation, state-tracking with rewards, and auditory-visual classification, using both theoretical and real neurobiological parameters.
By showing the efficacy of minimal neural systems, we've taken a step forward in understanding how biological brains efficiently learn and make decisions.

Researchers initially developed the geometric categority of finitely generated algebras in the late 1990s. This non-computational approach was initially applied to commutative algebras and later extended to associative and Lie algebras independently. The main goal of this paper is to introduce a new geometric categority for nilpotent algebras, which is more fundamental than the existing ones. Building upon previous research and incorporating recent advances in algebraic techniques, we define a geometric categority that can differentiate between isomorphic nilpotent algebras with distinct presentations. The study further establishes key mathematical connections, including a precise relationship between the geometric categority and the algebraic shifted grading framework.

Active galactic nuclei with extremely powerful jets are among the brightest objects in the universe, their brightness fueled by supermassive black holes. Research suggests these objects can be seen from vast distances, their presence indicated by radio signals that can travel further than other forms of radiation. Although these sources are thought to be less common, their exceptional brightness means they are well-documented. In order to understand how these objects form and change over time, researchers have created detailed computer models that simulate the impact of magnetic fields in the jets. These models assume the presence of a luminous accretion disk surrounding a massive black hole, influenced by gas flowing in from surrounding disks and clouds. In a recent study, researchers explored how these magnetic field influences affect the growth of these objects, primarily consisting of matter flowing into a central black hole and powered by massive clouds in the surrounding environment. In a recent addition to this research, scientists have used detailed computer models to investigate how cosmic background radiation affects these objects, particularly their appearance and the presence of jets powered by matter moving at relativistic speeds. To expand on this, researchers have used a computer model to investigate how, at redshift levels exceeding 6, radiation from the cosmic background affects the growth of these objects, particularly the presence of high-speed jets. In a recent study, researchers examined the effects of background radiation on these objects, specifically their appearance and the presence of high-speed jets, using computer models that incorporate the influence of magnetic fields in the jets and the structure

Classical gravity's Lagrangian, when considering falling bodies, has a well-established formulation as the difference between kinetic and potential energy. However, this simple approach fails to yield a well-defined Lagrangian for general relativity, due to its geometric nature. Despite this, there are alternative geometric representations of classical gravity that maintain a geometric interpretation similar to the original Einstein's theory. In this article, we explore these modifications to the Lagrangian for classical gravity.

This study introduces an unsupervised image matching technique that utilizes symmetric patterns in a point cloud to calculate distances and establish correspondences between volumes. A novel feature descriptor leverages local pre-image symmetry, eliminating the need for pre-computation like in other symmetric distance methods. Instead, symmetry is detected post-image matching. Once the 3D point cloud is created, the technique employs a symmetric distance metric to calculate optimal correspondences between two volumes, also taking into account dual and inverted patterns. A comprehensive evaluation of our method demonstrates its effectiveness and efficiency against a challenging dataset of 59 volumetric models. Furthermore, this study proposes a symmetrical extension of the well-known ICP algorithm, aiming to improve 3D image registration, but this variant proves less effective in our evaluation.

We've analyzed the data from the SDSS J082239.54+304857.19 double-degenerate binary system, focusing on its unusual 40.5 minutes eclipses which feature distinct variations in low-frequency and high-frequency waves. After conducting an extensive search, we identified three distinct sinusoidal patterns associated with these eclipses - each with unique frequencies and amplitudes. Through our calculations, we determined that these rhythms result from the interaction of second and fourth harmonic components of the primary oscillations, triggered by the system's orbital movement around its axis. Based on our findings, we calculated the system's critical parameters, such as the orbital period and inclination, as well as the inherent oscillation period. We theorize that the observed variations in this binary system can be attributed to nonlinear effects resulting from the system's complex geometry and the super-Earth/mini-Neptune host star's extensive atmospheric layers.

This study re-inspects global aggregation techniques in light of Optimal Transport theory, and suggests a novel approach to aggregation problems that takes into account varying domain sizes. By formulating global aggregation as an OT-problem, we can leverage existing solutions and yield frameworks for multiple tasks like image categorization and object detection. Our proposed method is illustrated using a simple "counting-people" task and a more complex full-body human pose estimation challenge.

This investigation delves into the host galaxies of five distinct AGN subclasses which emit gamma-rays, namely BL Lac, BL PG, Seyfert, NL and LINER. To determine the host galaxies, we utilized NICI and HST archival images to isolate the galactic core and estimate the intrinsic luminosity, color and size for each class. Additionally, we calculated the ratio of host to bright nuclear emission in the near infrared for all sampled galaxies. Our analysis reveals significant differences in inclination between gamma-ray BL Lac and NL/ LINER Seyfert galaxies, while no variation was found in the size and color of their host galaxies. In contrast, the host galaxies of BL Lac and PG galaxies exhibit noticeable signs of Seth et al.'s host galaxy evolution. This research suggests that the AGN subclasses studied are not associated with varying host galaxy types, but rather differ in the orientation of the galactic disc due to the nature of the AGN emission.

This research paper focuses on finding a novel flat rotational plane in the Euclidean space E4, defined by a specific geometric structure that involves a 1-type Gauss function. Employing an invariant approach, we establish that conditions for this structural consistency are fulfilled when an appropriate scalar curvature condition is met. Subsequently, we select a specific geometric configuration that satisfies this condition, resulting in a specific example of flat rotational plane.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires extensive annotation for segmentation masks, making it a labor-intensive task. Researchers have found that preruning their models on depth estimation or 3D object recognition can significantly reduce the annotation cost. However, whether depth estimation can serve as an effective precursor for semantic segmentation has yet to be confirmed. Previous studies on preruning for semantic segmentation have largely relied on monocular depth estimation as a pre-training method, but they have not thoroughly evaluated its effectiveness. Our research reveals that monocular depth estimation is not always a reliable pre-training method compared to object recognition. When monocular depth estimation is used as pre-training, it can actually hinder the performance of the model, making it harder to converge. Our study also identifies the reason for this poor performance and proposes a solution to improve convergence, highlighting the limitations of monocular depth estimation as a pre-training method.

This work focuses on generating time-series narratives that incorporate various
domain-specific elements. Current narrative generation models, however, often
require pre-trained language models and are typically applied to a single domain.
We introduce TCube, a novel neural narrative generation model that can seamlessly
switch between different domains without requiring re-training. TCube uses a
knowledge graph to create stories by interacting with the graph as if it's a
three-dimensional cube. We evaluate TCube's performance on three domains and
find that it surpasses the existing models trained on a single domain. Moreover,
our analysis demonstrates that TCube's ability to transition between domains is
not a result of its exposure to common domain-neutral time-series patterns.

The ATLAS experiment examines unusual phenomena and CP violation in beauty mesons utilizing proton-proton collision data collected at 7 and 8 TeV. This study investigates the following processes: $B^0_s \to J/\psi\mu^+\mu^-$ in $B^0_s^{\ast+}$ decays, $B^0_s \to D^{\ast+} D^-\mu^+\mu^-$, and various occurrences of $B^0 \to D^{\ast+} D^-$ and $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$ decays.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation.

This research explores the global solvability of certain partial differential equations, specifically those belonging to the category of sublogarithmic $p$-PDEs, given the constraints of $1 \leq p < 2$. These equations are represented by the partial differential equation $\frac{\partial}{\partial t} (u^{p-1}) = A(u)$ in the context of Hilbert space $H$, with $A$ denoted as a smooth, analytic dissipative olomorphic operator. Establishing the requirements for global well-posedness, we examine multiple scenarios involving the properties of $p$, the geometry of $H$, and the behavior of $A$, while providing several illustrative examples that satisfy these conditions. Notably, we analyze cases where $p$ is close to 2, but less than, equal to 2 from below.

This study introduces Enhanced ESTIMATES, an improved version of the ESTIMATES model, for solving the Japanese word division problem. The original ESTIMATES model used an attention-based neural network to predict word divisions based on character models, contextual information, and phonic patterns. However, it suffered from a limited training capacity of 40,000 characters. To overcome this limitation, we developed the Enhanced ESTIMATES model, which leverages pre-trained neural networks using a confidence-based sampling method. The model was trained on a comprehensive dataset of 178,000 characters and demonstrated superior performance in prediction accuracy and coverage. Furthermore, we developed a system integrating Enhanced ESTIMATES with a leading Japanese NLP engine to achieve a 95.6% division accuracy in a real-world application.

On the Stack Overflow platform, users engage with over 13 million questions daily, sharing 40,000+ answers and nearly 1 million external links. These links, associated with answers, provide users with additional information and can serve as a means to monitor and understand the flow of external information shared within the community. This study analyzes the most frequently shared domains among Stack Overflow questions, revealing over 215,000 distinct domains associated with 18 million answers. Following data collection, the most prevalent domains were examined, and analysis indicated that the most frequently shared external sources on Stack Overflow include documentation for software development related to Microsoft and Adobe, as well as official tutorials and blogs. Our findings show that the most active question askers tend to be associated with the most external links, and these activities correlate positively with reputation growth.

The stability of galaxies has been a persistent issue in astrophysics for decades, with numerous studies attempting to provide a definitive answer. In this study, we will re-examine potential explanations for galaxy stability, including the 'Gaseous Disk Solution,' 'Mass Inflow Solution,' and 'Dark Matter Solution,' and evaluate which of these options shows the most promise based on current scientific knowledge. Conversely, we will rule out the 'Baryonically Efficient Solution' as an unlikely explanation for galaxy stability due to its inadequacies. Ultimately, our findings will highlight the critical role that dark matter plays in maintaining the stability of galaxies, consistent with a wide range of observational evidence in astrophysics and cosmology.

To address climate change, nations must engage in productive discussions and 
implementing meaningful policies, yet global climate talks often face significant 
challenges, including economies with incompatible climate views. Developing and 
industrial nations frequently clash due to conflicting time constraints, and 
existing information gaps hindering climate understanding. Therefore, there is a 
need to enhance climate negotiations through data-driven insights, and our proposed 
Climate Knowledge Repository (CKR) aims to bridge information gaps among nations, 
addressing key data missing links in climate discussions. By establishing the 
CKR, we imported open-source climate data, leveraged data mining techniques for 
exploration and analysis, and applied natural language processing to facilitate 
effective knowledge sharing among participating nations. Our case study with the 
Government of Malaysia demonstrates the CKR's capability in identifying trends and 
connections with global partners, and we envision the CKR to serve as a reference 
point for nations in similar positions, enabling them to make more informed policy 
decisions based on objective climate context comparisons with international 
partners.

Medical researchers and clinicians heavily rely on thoroughly annotated patient data to make informed decisions. Nevertheless, obtaining these annotations proves to be a daunting task due to the resource-intensive process involved. This paper presents a novel approach to overcome the limitation of data availability by facilitating domain generalization through adaptation. We focus on extracting essential information related to patient symptoms from medical notes, aiming to achieve this cross-domain with minimal adaptation through our proposed method. We evaluated this approach using various clinical datasets and found that it efficiently crosses boundaries between different domains with only a few adaptations. Moreover, our adapter-based model offers enhanced adaptability and a straightforward way to make predictions in unfamiliar domains. We also demonstrated through ablation studies that each component of our adapter contributes significantly to its effectiveness. We openly provide our data, code, and adapter-fine-tuned models on our GitHub repository and the models on Hugging Face Datasets repository for reproducibility purposes.

Deep reinforcement learning has gained significant attention in the intelligent transportation system due to its ability to learn tasks within complex environments. The following text will examine the application of deep reinforcement learning in the development of self-driving cars, focusing on categorical scenarios such as navigation, collision avoidance, and route selection. Categorical scenarios are those with multiple potential outcomes based on different actions taken.

For self-driving vehicles, reinforcement learning offers a direct approach to mapping controller inputs to outcomes. Typically, the behavior of self-driving cars is described through a triple (S, A, R), comprising a set of states (S), possible actions (A), and immediate rewards (R). However, this framework poses a challenge as most states are non-discrete, leading to the infinite dimensionality of actions and rewards. This issue is mitigated by deep reinforcement learning models using function approximation.

One such model, the Self-Driving Controller (SDC), was presented in a 2020 study. It employed a neural network to learn the mapping between states and actions, mapping states to actions in the 3D autonomous vehicle control space. The controller was trained using a dataset of 80,000 simulated states. The model was tested in two scenarios and compared to existing vehicle control methods, demonstrating its effectiveness through its integration in the Autoworld project. 

Another model, the Deep Neural Network-based Controller (DNC), was introduced in a 2021 study. It expanded upon the SDC by mapping states to a discrete set of actions

Deep neural networks excel in image classification, yet their significant computational resources and substantial model size pose significant challenges. In response to these issues, researchers have advocated for spiking neural networks due to their potential for substantial energy reductions. However, the randomness in synapses and neurons within the system introduces uncertainty in processing delays, which complicates the timely coordination of spike transmission. Consequently, the efficiency of energy-efficient spiking neural networks is hindered. In this study, we present an innovative random synapse model and develop a novel training algorithm utilizing an evolutionary technique to optimize the network's accuracy and energy consumption. The experimental outcomes, applied to image classification on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets, demonstrate that our method maintains the high accuracy of state-of-the-art CNNs while achieving substantial energy savings comparable to those of Neo-Caris, a renowned spiking neural network. Notably, our method surpasses Neo-Caris in energy efficiency by as much as 2.16 times while maintaining similar accuracy. Moreover, our results show that the resulting RNNs comprise 97.86% fewer parameters than those of Charis, a renowned spiking neural network, without compromising accuracy.

This research investigates the characteristics of a quark star made up of spin-aligned quarks under the influence of intense magnetic fields, all of which are variable. By employing the MIT bag model, we were able to derive equations of state, discover maximum mass limits, and learn how temperature and magnetic fields impact a quark star's overall structure. Our outcomes demonstrate that a quark star composed of spin-aligned quarks can endure extreme external forces, including strong magnetic fields, which is significant for understanding objects in dense stellar environments.

A rapidly growing network of nearly 800 million PCs is accessible through standard web browsers, enabling a vast potential for computational power to be harnessed. To unlock this potential, a new system called Pando has been created, allowing developers to write and execute parallel applications under a shared, decentralized architecture. By integrating a common programming language with advanced data structures, developers can now construct applications that utilize the collective computing power of this vast network, while maintaining security through robust software protection and distributed compilation. Initially implemented with the C language and later with other languages, Pando has successfully run a range of computational intensive applications including video encoding, molecular simulations, and quantum calculations, outperforming faster machines by utilizing the collective power of many computers. The effectiveness and efficiency of Pando have been further demonstrated in a series of comprehensive benchmarks, showcasing its capability to effectively distribute application computation across the vast distributed computing network.

This research explores an estimation technique for nonlinear eigenvalues and eigenvectors that involves interpolating a model based on minimal rational functions. When estimating a linear model, this approach mirrors the Lasso method by employing a least squares minimization with an additional regularization term. In the context of nonlinear estimation, this technique can be associated with an L1-regularized minimization of a metric, specifically the Cressie-Read family, under influence of parameters λ and ρ. Results indicate that as the regularization parameters approach zero, the estimates converge to the exact eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and that for small values of these parameters, the estimates depend on the eigenvalues of a nonlinear matrix operator. Moreover, a selection technique for the above-mentioned parameters was developed, allowing adaptation to data, and evidence of convergence to the exact eigenvectors and eigenvalues is present in the asymptotic behavior. Numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this technique, and it successfully recovers nonlinear components in synthetic and real-world data sets.

We develop a model for intermediate beta-transformations with a gap, resulting in two scenarios: the transform has a fixed point when the gap is excluded, or the gap serves as a scaling interval. Within this framework, we demonstrate the creation of Hausdorff biographies—collections of closed intervals—and associated Cantor sets, ultimately linking them to the dynamic properties of certain beta-transformations.

In this brief communication, we provide evidence that certain $SO(N_c)$ gauge theories become confined with a large number of colors $N_c$, exhibiting a IR phase with completely broken chiral symmetry. We offer a detailed explanation using the'simplest' vector operator, $\mathbf{6}_s$, within the lattice regularization framework. We demonstrate, both numerically and analytically, that the symmetric subset of the relevant set of baryon-like operators systematically decreases as the lattice gauge coupling increases, much like in $SU(N_f)$ Yang-Mills theory. Notably, in contrast to theories formed by Yang-Mills, we find a fully broken chiral symmetry in the confined phase, marked by a significant drop of the composite boson dimension $\delta\tilde{d}$, instead of a gradual decrease. This breakage is accompanied by the emergence of massless 'baryon' modes in the lattice, resulting from the dimensionality transformation of the $\mathbf{6}_s \times \mathbf{6}_s$ instanton. Additionally, we show that the fully broken chiral symmetry, accompanied by the confinement, is signified by the appearance of massive'meson' modes on the lattice, formed by the fusion of the 'baryon' ones.

Machine learning models such as Random Forest and Boosted Trees have wide-ranging applications, yet their intricate structure makes it difficult to understand their decision-making processes. Our proposed method, Disentangled Attribution Graphs, provides transparent and accountable explanations for these models by visually illustrating how input variables contribute to each prediction outcome. Our method is adaptable to various tree-based models, including their ensemble versions, and showcases its effectiveness through successful applications in multiple domains.

In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, such as using secure multiparty computation and trusted execution environments (TEEs), have introduced new attacks vectors and complexities. This paper presents a new framework, Flatee, that offers a simplified and efficient solution for collaborative training within TEEs. Flatee's key features include interleaving encryption and compression to minimize computational and communication overheads, and a new degree-of-trust metric that enables parties to control security trade-offs. Our results show that Flatee achieves significantly faster communication times compared to previous TEE-based solutions, with a performance improvement of up to 2.5 times. Additionally, Flatee's overheads enable secure training on models that TEE-based approaches could only accomplish with significantly larger datasets. For example, Flatee enabled secure collaboration on a dataset that was 20 times smaller than what was required for a comparable TEE-based approach.

This research introduces a cost-effective solution for evaluating industrial automation operators on embedded systems with limited resources. Despite the widespread use of touchscreens in modern automation, comprehensive testing of interactive applications remains a significant challenge. To address this issue, we have developed a modular testing framework that can run on hardware-independent targets and provide automated verification of visual and touch interactions. This approach consists of an automated touch emulator, capable of mimicking real-world user inputs on a touchscreen device. By leveraging this emulator, developers can create automated test cases that align with real-world user scenarios, enabling thorough testing of complex industrial automation applications.

This research introduces Timeloops, a proactive container management approach that learns system call policies for microservices and adapts to new service patterns without human intervention.  Timeloops uses a machine learning-based method to develop these policies, which are refined in real-time by analyzing the system's temporal relationships and adapting to changes.  This technique also incorporates sequential techniques to efficiently handle large amounts of data from containerized systems. 

In contrast to existing methods, Timeloops directly learns policies from observed data rather than relying on expert knowledge or theoretical models.  This involves analyzing the underlying dynamics of the system and identifying causes and effects through the study of temporal relationships.  Furthermore, Timeloops's adaptive nature allows it to respond to unexpected events and evolving system patterns without disrupting the service.  This has been verified through experiments using a production-ready microservices platform, which demonstrated that Timeloops can learn effective system call policies more quickly and with less data than traditional methods, while also reducing the risk of errors and downtime during the policy development process.

One of the primary goals in differential geometry involves determining the conditions under which linear functions can be represented as metric projections in Euclidean, hyperbolic, or spherical spaces. Achieving classification with linear models in these spaces requires establishing the uniqueness of linear projections, which in turn relies on the separation theorem. In this research, we investigate the feasibility of linear classifiers in Euclidean, hyperbolic, and spherical spaces of dimension $d \geq 2$. Our study reveals that linear classifiers are capable in the Euclidean space but fail in the hyperbolic and spherical spaces due to the presence of closed loops and spheres that encompass all points in those manifolds. To address these challenges, we develop novel techniques for creating pseudo-dimension and establish the VC dimension for linear classifiers in the hyperbolic and spherical spaces. Our research also explores the creation of pseudo-dimension for linear models through the use of random features and Fourier coefficients.

This work revisits the scenario of stars orbiting around a massive black hole at the center of a galaxy, focusing specifically on the region where stars have highly elliptical orbits. Even though existing research has thoroughly analyzed the behavior of stars in this area, the current study seeks to address a question left unanswered by previous work: how do the predictions of the collisionless approximation hold up for stars with highly eccentric orbits that take them very close to the central black hole? In general, the accuracy of these predictions depends on the amount of energy each star expends during its journey and can be quantified by the change in its orbital frequency, known as $\Delta \bar{\nu}$. This value serves as a measure of how strongly the gravitational influence of surrounding stars affects each stellar orbit. Previous estimates suggest that the collisionless regime remains valid for stars with less elliptical orbits, but for those with highly elliptical paths, the question persists as to what factors lead to the invalidation of these predictions and what factors indicate the strict application of the collisionless theory. Building on previous work, the current study develops a method to determine when the collisionless regime is relevant and introduces a new concept, called "stellar arrangement parameters", to classify different star configurations based on their orbital patterns. By analyzing various scenarios of stellar distributions, the research demonstrates that the standard collisionless model is sufficient for stars with certain characteristics but that more nuanced modeling is necessary for others, and proposes a framework for evaluating when enhanced modeling is necessary.

A chronological method known as sequential decision making, utilizing sequences of random actions, can be followed to make (random) decisions. Building on this, the strategy of sequential decision making can be modified to account for uncertainties by creating multiple sequences of random actions in advance. This paper presents a basic framework for managing a system that produces output over time based on prior observations and available actions, with the goal of minimizing costs. A simple example illustrates the application of this framework in a realistic setting.

Independent Component Analysis is a fundamental technique for uncovering hidden patterns in data, yet its applications are largely limited to non-critical scenarios due to the high computational demands and fragile stability of the underlying algorithms. Our research focuses on developing robust and efficient analysis methods for complex, high-dimensional data sets characterized by non-Gaussian distributions and varying densities. The novel algorithms we present maintain a linear model, where the components can be rotated, and are based on optimization principles, utilizing specific properties of the data (moments, correlations) to uncover the underlying structures. The ease of computation, enhanced stability, and reduced estimation errors of these algorithms make them suitable for high-dimensional data analysis. The theoretical foundations of our approach, grounded in the principles of Compressive Sensing, allow our methods to achieve optimal information recovery with minimal data access. The efficiency of our algorithms is further exemplified by experiments using artificial and real-world data sets.

A species model incorporating a competition-colonization tradeoff has been created, where species disseminate through chaotic dynamics and competitive interactions. This model has been proven to be a species interaction model with a confirmed species coexistence theorem in a particular setting. However, our research reveals that this model doesn't consistently guarantee coexistence. We've found species elimination scenarios in environments with three or four species. Our analysis provides a comprehensive study of the model's species dynamics and offers valuable insights into species coexistence and extinction. It's noteworthy that this model shares similarities with the chaotic voter model, yet shows distinct behavior unlike previously reported results for that model.

The category of regional von Neumann algebras plays a crucial role in establishing duality at the non-perturbative level of the abelian quantum double model. Similar to the behavior in the haag-dombey model, the non-degenerate extension of the algebra and regional von Neumann algebras in the abqdm form a monoidal category that is symmetric and brazeily equipped with a functor that represents the passage from a region to its temporal shift. Additionally, the category of regional von Neumann algebras in the abqdm has been proven to be equivalent to the category of von Neumann algebras formed from wightman structures representing local states.

To enhance the magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in a cavity magnomechanics system, we introduce a coherent feedback circuit that facilitates real-time interaction between the magnon, photon, and phonon modes. 

From a quantum theory perspective, we have analyzed the time-evolved density matrices for the hybridized modes, and discovered that the inclusion of coherent feedback results in increased entanglement between the modes, as well as improved stability.

Our numerical simulations demonstrate the quantifiable advantages of this approach, specifically by optimizing the phonon-bright magnon states and maximizing the tri-mode entanglement.

Ultimately, our findings showcase the efficacy of coherent feedback in a cavity magnomechanics system for generating highly entangled states, thereby expanding the utility of this platform for various quantum information applications and research in quantum physics.

We've completed a thorough compilation of one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for QCD, using a dimensionally-regularized framework. Our work builds upon previous research and employs an effective technique to remove spurious divergences, allowing us to derive exact expressions for all relevant splitting operators. We've specifically obtained precise formulas for double- and single-spacetime-dimensional cases. Moreover, we've directly extracted all soft and double-soft operators from our results. We've also provided an alternative expression for the $\mathcal{F}_{qq'}/2$ splitting function from a different perspective, featuring a simpler form without complex coefficients.

Let $R$ be a one-dimensional local ring with residue field $k$ and index of nilpotency $v$, and consider the category ${\rm PosNrd_+}(R)$ consisting of positive Neron desingularization functors that maintain positivity. When $R$ has a $k$-freeness property, a universal Neron desingularization ${\rm UnNrd}_R$ exists within this category, and it represents a class of "good" desingularization functors that preserve $R$-algebraic properties. Moreover, we define a version of the universal Neron desingularization for a finite collection $R_i, i=1,\ldots,n$ of one-dimensional local rings and establish its existence in the specific case where each ring $R_i$ shares the same residue field $k$.

The proliferation of smartphones has rendered analog devices like sundials obsolete, 
rendering them unused and unloved. Consequently, the art of sundial manufacturing has 
decreased, causing a shortage of skilled craftsmen. To revive interest in this ancient 
technology, the Suryakala-Nusantara project was launched. It documented 132 sundials from 
across Indonesia and introduced a new line of modern sundials, introducing a novel 
application. Researchers collected data from both ancient and modern sundials, 
investigating their functional possibilities. By combining this data with computational 
tools, they were able to simulate and visualize each sundial's functional trajectory 
throughout the year, obtaining essential metrics. A mobile app for Android devices was 
also developed, enabling users to identify sundials, view their functions, and verify 
data collected by the Suryakala-Nusantara team. A comprehensive website provides 
access to the collected data, results, and other project resources. The team is now 
recruiting volunteers to verify the accuracy of the data and develop a community of 
interested sundial enthusiasts.

Artificial intelligence (AI) reflects the intellect of future intelligent societies, thus, developing intelligent networks with coexisting AI and D2D (Device-to-Device) communications is crucial. A novel surface-aided integrated information framework combines AI and D2D communications to create an AI-intuitive network reflecting human intellect. This surface-aided integrated information framework consists of a higher-order thinking area, a lower-order execution area, and a neural-like interaction mechanism. A mini-game interactive model demonstrates that its information framework approaches human intellect when the surface-to-brain signal delay is minimal. This minimal delay is calculated based on the integrated information metric. To minimize this delay, an online energy-efficient optimization algorithm is developed, allowing AI and D2D communications to interact and adapt through a two-and-a-half-layer neural network. This interaction enables the removal of redundant interactions between D2D nodes, thus, increasing the integrated information metric. This surface-aided integrated information framework outperforms current surface-aided and neural networking frameworks, thus, making them redundant. This intelligent artificial intelligence framework is universal, thus, applicable to any surface-aided and neural networking scenarios.

The effectiveness of Laser Doppler Velocimetry (LDV) in gathering high-resolution, individual-particle velocity data is well-established. Recent research has highlighted its potential in quantitative fluid flow analysis.
