The application of advanced machine learning methods to vast astronomical datasets is hindered by their computational intensity, making them impractical to execute using traditional high-performance computer architectures due to data randomness and the need for repetitive computations. Our research demonstrates how these issues can be overcome through the implementation of a photonic flow-based network, a type of generative model, to solve the spectral cross-matching problem. This novel approach offers two main advantages: it enables the creation of an adaptable, hardware-independent binary code for mapping unknown spectra to reference spectra, and it facilitates the incorporation of complex astronomical spectral features into its structure. Our photonic network outperforms existing methods in accuracy and exhibits an impressive 97.5% precision in identifying known spectra and 95.5% precision in identifying unknown spectra. Additionally, its predictive code is highly resilient to errors and can be rapidly generated at the point of use. These features make this photonic design an ideal solution for processing massive astronomical datasets, addressing challenges related to data size, complexity, and real-time labeling. Our work also enables the incorporation of light-based data reading and processing capabilities, enabling the development of versatile, reliable, and fast photonic solutions for spectral cross-matching.

In the pharmaceutical sector, numerous medications interact in intricate ways, influencing each other's effects, either augmenting or diminishing their outcomes. These interactions have significant implications for treatment strategies, yet the current understanding of them is limited. To rectify this, we develop a novel score-based framework to assess medication pair relationships. Our approach, which combines relational learning with a scoring system, assigns a numerical value to each medication pair, reflecting the intensity of their interactions. By employing the RePTN network, a relational graph convolutional neural network, we can obtain fine-grained, dose-dependent interaction details. Additionally, our framework incorporates auxiliary tasks in an adversarial manner and uses a cumulative proportional loss function to enhance training efficiency. Our results, based on an analysis of existing case reports, demonstrate the capability of our framework to accurately predict real-world medication pair relationships.

Automated driving systems are now prevalent and their demand is rising rapidly worldwide. To enhance vehicle safety, there's a pressing need for a broad automated driving function that can identify and adapt to various roads across different countries. Currently, most advanced road recognition systems are only effective within a single country, hindering their expansion to new markets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a unified framework that can recognize and classify roads in multiple nations. Our approach integrates transfer learning with a dynamic road harm detection model to facilitate adaptation to new environments. Our model's performance has been thoroughly evaluated using a massive dataset of 226,000 images gathered from multiple sources, representing roads in good and poor condition. Our results demonstrate that our model can accurately identify and classify roads in multiple nations without extensive retraining, showcasing its versatility and efficiency.

Our primary objective is to develop a method to learn policies across various areas without needing targeted training in those specific areas. Given access to videos tagged with intentions in one domain, our algorithm generates policies in a second, distinct domain, where videos are also labeled. The only requirement is that both domains feature optical character recognition (OCR) capabilities to extract intent-related text data. The policy learned through our method can accurately navigate to the intended location in the new domain, as demonstrated by experiments on navigating to focused intent objects in two distinct domains. The source code for our project can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ghuntley/CAIO

Intensifying the magnetic field surrounding a Population III protostar has been found to prevent the formation of a protoplanetary disk, according to a simulation using the FLASH code for radiative transfer and astrophysical fluids, with a 3D MHD framework. This outcome resulted from the intensified magnetic field threading through and interacting with a surrounding gas cloud that had undergone collapse, leading to the development of a dynamically significant magnetized disk. However, in models with the highest magnetic field intensification levels (8-32 times the standard value), the magnetic field dominated disk fragmented into multiple planets due to instabilities, with up to 12 distinct planetary masses emerging. Ultimately, the intensified magnetic field prevented the formation of a protoplanetary disk by suppressing the development of a disk with a small radial mass distribution and by inhibiting the fragmentation of the disk.

In the context of data mining, researchers often utilize complex association rule analysis by leveraging formal concepts linked to lattice structures and frameworks for automatic theorem proving. This study explores how repetition affects the results of data sets when translated into mathematical frameworks. We demonstrate that, from a theoretical standpoint, there are data sets for which the number of required transactions to form a given association rule depends on the minimum size of the rule's base within a lattice. To support our findings, we provide examples of data sets that illustrate how the number of transactions can vary according to the rule's base size. Additionally, we propose algorithms to determine the least sized bases for a given dataset and associate them with the lowest binding powers in a Galois framework. We also examine how various parameters, such as the level of confidence and difference thresholds, influence the performance of our designed heuristics and present results of extensive testing on artificially created datasets.

Following the passage of Proposition 63 in November 2014, California mandated court-ordered therapy for individuals convicted of non-violent crimes. Our study examines how this treatment impacted the mental well-being of those convicted, particularly exploring the effects on symptoms of anxiety and depression. Notably, we discovered significant variations in treatment outcomes based on the type of therapy provided, with certain approaches resulting in reduced symptoms of anxiety and others lessening symptoms of depression. Our analysis also uncovers the profound impact of peer support groups, leading to notable decreases in both anxiety and depression symptoms. These findings indicate that leveraging peer support groups within treatment can be beneficial in reducing symptoms among individuals convicted of non-violent crimes, thus contributing to a safer and more productive reintegration into society.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and investigate special cases, including connections to Bernoulli polynomials.

Radio maps are gaining traction as a means to understand and navigate wireless communication, providing insight into signal strength and patterns that can inform device location, configuration, and operation. Although radio maps have been primarily computed through systematic field measurements, their primary limitation is the need to return to the base after each measurement, rendering the process slow and unproductive. This paper introduces an innovative approach to rapidly construct radio maps using drones. By equipping the drone with a wireless wide area network receiver, the flight path is recorded alongside the collected signal strength data. This process creates a map of signal strength, but it lacks precise location accuracy due to the limitations of simple GPS. This issue is resolved by taking the radio map, including the drone's recorded path, to a machine learning algorithm that employs geographic self-supervised learning to generate locations for any point in the environment. This method produces accurate results, rivaling the effectiveness of traditional radio map surveying methods. Furthermore, the approach enables previously unachievable efficiency, reducing the time required to construct the radio map.

This research introduces an innovative method using Hidden Markov Models to evaluate job candidate interview recordings and identify anomalies. Anomalous clips are detected by comparing predicted and actual gauge probabilities, revealing problematic sections. Anomaly severity is quantified through the gauge probability error, which correlates with conversational abnormalities. This approach enables automated anomaly detection, facilitating manual review and reducing the complexity of the process. Unlike other techniques that rely on rule-based methods or natural language processing, this method uses a probabilistic approach to improve scalability and adaptability.

This study investigates the effectiveness of a robust authentication system combining audio, visual, and thermal signatures. It involves analyzing and combining the unique features of these signatures to enhance authentication capabilities. Experimental results on a created database reveal a top-notch performance with a 99.1% accuracy rate for speaker recognition, a 100% accuracy rate for face recognition, and a 100% accuracy rate for authentication using thermal signatures. Furthermore, a security breach examination and performance evaluation under various noise conditions are conducted to demonstrate the strength and robustness of this authentication system.

Current state-of-the-art automatic speech recognition and translation systems are highly effective but necessitate substantial training data, which can be impractical to obtain. We introduce an innovative, low-effort approach to boost recognition accuracy by leveraging unlabelled audio, translation, and other related data. This method enhances the recognition model through a data augmentation technique that minimally modifies existing speech data with acoustic and translation features. Our experiments on the LibriSpeech 30-hour dataset and the IWSLT 15 English-to-Spanish translation dataset demonstrate remarkable success, with our method outperforming baseline performance by a significant 9.5% and 2.1% respectively, using labels alone, or 5.5% and 1.3% using labels and small amounts of human-labeled data.

Consider a mixture of $K$ distinct populations, each characterized by a normal distribution with unknown mean $\mu_k$ and standard deviation $\sigma_k$.  We seek to estimate the average of the population means, denoted as $\bar{\mu}$, alongside the standard deviations $\sigma_k$, given a set of independent, randomly drawn samples, each from one of the populations.  Our approach provides reliable estimates of the population means and standard deviations under two scenarios: when the means and variances are known for all populations, or when only the variances are known.  The method is then applied to construct confidence intervals for the population means, enabling comparisons with existing large-sample methods.  The proposed method is thoroughly validated through simulations, which further illustrate its applicability to sampling scenarios.

Achieving confidentiality in private databases has become a significant concern. Previously, a framework called Differential Privacy (DP) was established to ensure this confidentiality, where an adversary is restricted from accessing sensitive information by gradually deprioritizing relevant data. However, this approach has several drawbacks as it may result in inaccurate outcomes and reduced efficiency. One-Sided DP (ODP) was created to address these issues in certain scenarios, however, there is a gap in research regarding the development of efficient methods for ODP. This study introduces a novel technique for ODP that guarantees a specific level of protection, DP, over releasing multiple datasets while accounting for potential dependencies within these datasets. This has implications in various fields such as statistics and machine learning. The research focuses on measuring confidentiality breaches related to specific characteristics within the datasets. This work also introduces a mathematical assessment for determining the likelihood and severity of confidentiality breaches. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of this technique through numerical examples.

In AS 209, a mature protoplanetary system with a 7-magnitude star and 3 detectable planets, researchers analyze the organic molecules CO, CCH, and CCS within a 200 AU by 200 AU field of view. They discover that the organic molecules reside within the CO gas gap at the inner disk and exhibit lower abundance than outer counterparts. This decrease in abundance by a factor of 5 or more is consistent whether considering the inner or outer areas. Researchers explore two possible explanations for this organic molecule decline. First, that the inner areas' lower temperature and pressure enable more efficient formation of these molecules. Alternatively, that the inner areas are subject to destructive chemical processing by planetesimal surfaces or photochemistry. Due to a lack of current models, the data does not definitively support either theory. However, the organic molecule data, combined with the existing CO gas gap observations, suggests that the second scenario may be more consistent.

This research introduces an advanced toolset comprising several sub-tools that enable the examination of data sets with time markings in various scientific applications. Each of these sub-tools is designed to tackle a specific challenge associated with data analysis. The project's diverse range of tools are written in Python, a highly versatile programming language, and are therefore accessible to a broad user base. Like many open-source software projects, our toolset can be freely obtained from the Git repository, where users can also contribute new developments. Additionally, we have incorporated a user-friendly interface enabling quick data analysis by novice users who may not possess in-depth programming skills.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving controls with state limitations. 

Given a fixed probability measure $\mu_0$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, we define a class of probability measures $\mu_t$ evolving over time $t \geq 0$, such that each measure $\mu_t$ is associated with a control $u$ and has the same probability distribution as $\mu_0$. 

The cost function $F_t$ and the kernel $M_t$ are two functions of time $t$ and a variable $x$, whose properties ensure they are uniformly continuous and have specific properties. 

We represent the dynamics of the system using the following stochastic differential equation: 

$$
\begin{cases}
    dX_r = \sqrt{2} \bigl( \sqrt{F_r}(Y_r) + Z_r \bigr) dW_r, \\
    Z_r = M_r(X_r),
\end{cases}
$$

where $(W_r)_{r \geq 0}$ is a standard Wiener process, $(W_t)_{t \geq 0}$ is independent from $(X_r)_{r \geq 0}$ and $(Z_r)_{r \geq 0}$, and $(Y_r)_{r \geq 0}$ is a process representing the flow of measures $(\mu_r)_{r \geq 0

Studying stellar threads is crucial in understanding the nature of long, extended objects found in the Milky Way.  By analyzing these stellar threads, researchers aim to gain insights into the objects' formation, material distribution, and how they're projected against the background, all while accounting for the Gaia mission's precise data measurement capabilities.  The definition of a stellar thread, or filamentoide estelar, is initially examined and then reevaluated in light of the Gaia database.  Research on these stellar threads is further discussed, along with the objects' possible classification as mere aggregations of individual stars.  If these "stellar threads" are merely aggregates, then their analysis wouldn't offer unique or distinctive insights into the objects themselves, let alone their projected filamental appearance.

The pandemic has brought to light the importance of visual identification in the broader healthcare sector. Despite this, healthcare professionals often receive inadequate training on visual diagnosis, leading to gaps in their skills. Addressing this, our proposed solution, VICTOR, aims to streamline the visual identification process for healthcare professionals by facilitating the rapid verification of medical professionals' accurate visual diagnoses. By leveraging a combination of contrastive pre-training and fashion-specific fine-tuning, VICTOR shows exceptional performance in detecting discrepancies between the predicted image outputs of pre-trained models. Furthermore, our evaluation process, which incorporates both human assessment and numerical metrics, demonstrates VICTOR's clinical relevance and accuracy through its successful resolution of multiple clinical cases.

Quantum optics resources such as light quanta exhibit complex phenomena which are difficult to grasp through traditional quantum mechanics. Building on recent breakthroughs in quantum resource theory, a framework has been developed to characterize generalized nonclassical light, leveraging basic convex geometry methods. This informal review introduces key concepts from quantum resource theory, using real-time experiments to illustrate their relevance, before shifting to recent research on optical quantum systems. A focus is placed on recent findings regarding spatial coherence, quadrature entropy, and antinonclassical resources. This is followed by an examination of specific applications such as thermal states and $\chi$-superactivable states. Lastly, promising avenues for further investigation are identified.

As the need for distributed machine learning grows, federated learning has become a key framework for training models across multiple devices while maintaining data confidentiality. The Federated Learning ecosystem evolved over time with advancements such as asynchronous updates, allreduce, and buffered accumulation to address efficiency, latency, and uneven participant arrival and training durations. A critical challenge in federated learning lies in efficiently communicating the gradient update vector from participants to the aggregator. The current best practices involve participants waiting for their colleagues to update and the aggregator waiting for all participants to complete. This paper redefines the communication flow by allowing direct gradient transmission from participants to the aggregator at their respective update rates. We examine the effects of varying communication and computation imbalances on federated learning performance using a buffered asynchronous accumulation approach with a focus on the num\_acc accumulation parameter. The proposed solution is exemplified through a Keras-based implementation that demonstrates its efficacy and adaptability across various distributed learning scenarios.

The classical operational calculus developed by R. Graham and P. Butzer focuses on mapping polynomial functions over a test function space, such as Schwartz space or its variants, into distributions. In this study, we expand upon this concept by considering a more general function class, the set of polynomial tempered distributions, denoted as $\mathcal{D}_p^{\prime}$. We then establish a modified operational calculus, 'ad joint' operational calculus, by defining it as a mapping from the space $\mathcal{D}_p^{(j)}$ to $\mathcal{D}_p^{\prime}$, where $j$ and the differential sign denote differentiation. We also provide key theorems, including the 'ad joint' representation theorem and the 'ad joint' inversion theorem.

Building upon previous concepts, we introduce the Shadow Dimension, $D$, which represents an abstract space comprising collective shadowy images of fundamental matter particles. We propose that compact objects like stars and planets occupy a four-dimensional space-time framework, $S_4$, consisting of three spatial dimensions and one time dimension. We demonstrate how the Shadow Dimension, $D$, is intertwined with the number of scalar and vector fields in the low-energy effective theories of quantum states. We establish relationships between $D$ and characteristics of observational entities such as stars and the cosmic microwave background radiation. We show that in four-dimensional space-time frameworks, highly collapsed objects like primordial black holes have a Shadow Dimension of three, comprising one time and two spatial dimensions, aligned with the space-time framework occupied by fundamental matter particles. We determine the relationship between the Shadow Dimension and the number of matter fields in the universe and the scale of the Hubble constant, $\mathcal{H}$, within the context of the Dark Subluminous Universe Theory, revealing that primordial black holes in four-dimensional space-time frameworks adhere to the Swampland, satisfying the inequality, $m_{1/2} \leq \mathcal{H}$, with exceptions arising in instances of dark matter generation through phase transitions and instability decay. We derive a model-specific constraint, $m_{1/2} \leq 0.02\mathcal{H}$, applicable to primordial black holes in four-dimensional space-time

A floating raft is considered, with the area occupied by fractures modelled as a power-law distributed set of holes within the raft. It's observed that this fractal structure has a significant impact on the fractal geometry of cracks that form when the raft is subjected to an external load. This relationship is utilized to establish a correspondence between the dimensions of cracks and holes in the raft. It's noted that this method provides a general and applicable approach for studying both brittle and ductile materials, and a detailed mathematical representation of this relationship is presented.

The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. This issue arises due to the high density and anisotropic strain caused by the tetrahedral, hexagonal lattice structure difference between GaN and the group-IV nitrides MgSiN$_2$ and ZnGeN$_2$. To address this problem, we utilized a cutting technique to align the lattice structure of MgSiN$_2$ and ZnGeN$_2$ with that of GaN. Through this process, we enhanced the hole mobility in each material. Specifically, we observed improved mobility in ZnGeN$_2$/GaN, MgSiN$_2$/GaN, and MgSiN$_2$/ZnGeN$_2$ pseudosymmetrically engineered layers. We found that the strain-induced valence band hole mobility in each material could be increased by as much as five times. Moreover, we found that the hole mobility in each material could be optimally aligned vertically for optimal mobility. This discovery opens up new avenues for integrated gallium nitride electronics by addressing one of the field's persistent challenges.

Marine robots face significant challenges in navigating through complex coastal areas.
One critical issue is detecting and adapting to underwater currents, which can divert robots off-course.
Understanding the patterns and shifts of these currents over time is essential for effective navigation.
However, current methods are limited in their ability to learn and predict these patterns without extensive training or precise predictions.
These constraints make it difficult for robots to learn the space and time dynamics of the currents without being disrupted by distractions or inaccuracies.
A novel approach, Sparse Gaussian Process Regression, is proposed to learn and predict the patterns of coastal currents in real-time, using only a few actual data points and historical context.
The method is validated by comparing actual current measurements with its predictions on a well-documented coastal route, and the results show that SGPR accurately forecasts current patterns and helps marine robots achieve higher navigation accuracy and efficiency.

This research explores specific transformations, Darboux and Calapso, that can transform isothermal surfaces within a particular family, preserving their unique characteristics. We examine how these transformations affect the curvature properties of such surfaces in the context of a triholomorphic function. Additionally, a discussion on the constraints imposed by conservation laws is included, with a particular focus on how these transformations impact the curvature ellipse of the resulting surfaces.

This course note explores various methods for estimating a conditional expectation function (CEF) and associated its key characteristics, including its rate of convergence. We begin by examining the concept of almost sure convergence of certain estimation methods before delving into developing convergence rates and introducing influential work on adaptive estimation. Subsequent sections cover the development of least-squares estimators, a direct method of estimating CEFs, a method based on smoothing splines, and a method that incorporates orthogonal projections. We conclude by applying these estimation techniques to estimate conditional moments and correlate functions.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on modified joint generating functions of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second type, extending their work to $\lambda$-versions of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second type. We explore the relationships between $\lambda$-versions of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second type and other related numbers such as hypergeometric functions and core-stirling numbers, while also presenting a new recurrence relation for $\lambda$-versions of $r$-stirling numbers of the second type with a corresponding combinatorial interpretation.

Static knowledge graph frameworks are commonly used to link and forecast events in a static graph structure. Our research focuses on how to effectively utilize these frameworks, specifically by incorporating various techniques to boost link prediction accuracy for events. We believe that utilizing relevant information from surrounding events can aid in predicting future connections. Therefore, we developed two new methods: an average-based approach that aggregates and selects optimal links among adjacent events, and a threshold-based approach that identifies and exploits patterns of repeated relationship patterns. Experimental results demonstrate that these methods enhance the performance of static knowledge graph frameworks.

This note enhances and expands upon recent findings by Brown and the author, extending them to cover hereditary subcategories of row-finite graph C*-algebras, as well as a broader class of C*-algebras, in relation to a refined definition of shift equivalence.

Using the Keldysh-Sommerfeld perturbation theory, we investigated the transverse fragmentation function of a heavy quark hadron at finite magnetic and thermal conditions. By incorporating the pole mass scheme, we determined the irreducible self-energy contribution, which we then utilized to derive the self-energy and rescaled quark propagator at finite magnetic field. Our analysis demonstrated that in the presence of a strong magnetic field, heavy quark fragmentation behaves anisotropically, with fragmentation in the transverse direction being more preferred. Furthermore, we observed that as the magnetic field increases, heavy quark fragmentation becomes highly directional, which could potentially manifest in azimuthal asymmetries in particle spectra.

To overcome existing shortcomings in question answering models, particularly their inability to effectively utilize external knowledge and demonstrate domain expertise, we propose a new approach. It involves integrating a knowledge graph inference module to enhance each step of a multi-layer transformer language model. Each layer of the model is fed not only with the standard input, but also a simplified query derived from the question, along with its entity references, allowing the model to reason and select the most appropriate output from the contextualized word embeddings. Additionally, we develop a custom knowledge graph embedding model, KG-NCE, to produce more accurate knowledge graph embeddings that can be incorporated into the question answering framework. Experimental evaluations on the SQuAD dataset demonstrate the benefits of this multi-layer approach, with improvements in answer overlaps and accuracy scores across various question types. Most notably, the proposed model achieves the highest overall accuracy and performance in challenging scenarios, such as on data with missing context.

A high-dimensional expander graph is a high-dimensional combinatorial design with efficiently computable functions that produce distinct vertices given a random input. We develop a universal transformation that takes a low-dimensional expander graph and produces a high-dimensional one, maintaining the computational efficiency of the original functions. This achievement addresses two longstanding challenges in high-dimensional expander graphs: de Miloe's problem and the KMS conjecture, proposed respectively by Ben-David, Chor, and Sasson, and by Gromov, in 1983. Our construction relies on a deterministic covering of a high-dimensional geometric space by small-dimensional balls, which we refer to as a cover. A cover exhibits certain properties, including the following: it is non-trivial, efficient, compact, expansive, uniquely characteristic, and uniquely characteristic with proximity preservation. We apply our general approach by providing a new deterministic construction of balls for the Dyer-Franklin hypergraph, answering a question posed by Tewari and Vishwanathan. Furthermore, our results imply the creation of a high-dimensional expander graph whose functions have a query complexity of $O(\log n)$ and a spectral gap of $O(1)$, addressing a question posed by Ben-David, Chor, and Sasson.

To evaluate how task-specific various types of prompts are, we conducted
experiments using multiple new tasks. Our findings show that prompts based on
multiple choice are highly effective and can achieve impressive results with
minimal human input, requiring only one example for optimal performance. We
also discovered that multi-modal prompts which incorporate image information
yield superior outcomes to text-only prompts on more complex tasks. To enhance
the quality of automated prompts, we developed a new metric which evaluates
how task-specific a prompt is, demonstrating a significant correlation with
performance. We will be making our code and data available at https://github.com/aleksep/promt-assessment.

This note expands on the work of V. Royer and D. Benois by providing a generalized formula for p-adic L-functions in families, and subsequently derives a formula for the leading coefficients of these functions, leading to a computation of their critical values. This results in the determination of certain coefficients in the p-adic L-functions of Motives, a key part of the Fontaine-Mazur principle, and their critical values, which we term $\mathscr{L}$-invariants. This calculation also yields a formula for the normalized p-adic L-functions of Artin motives, and their leading coefficients.

Detecting subtle changes in microwave signals is crucial for various applications, including sensing and quantum computing. A technique known as Rydberg microwave detection has shown promise, leveraging Rydberg atoms' high sensitivity to radiation. Nonetheless, this approach has limitations when dealing with complex environments, as it demands significant signal-to-noise improvements. Conventionally, this has been achieved using frequency-modulated continuous wave detection, but this method has limitations in terms of detectable frequency ranges. A more versatile approach modulates only a portion of the signal and leaves the rest unmodulated, yet this configuration is susceptible to interference from sources like thermal noise. 

In our investigation, we employed this alternative RMD setup, coupled with advanced deep learning algorithms, to enhance its sensitivity to detectable frequencies. Through this combination, we significantly boosted the signal-to-noise ratio by approximately 20 decibels and 10 decibels for low and high power conditions, respectively. Our innovations have the potential to integrate seamlessly with current quantum technology platforms, leading to the development of more sophisticated quantum sensors and computers.

UGC 8839, an spiral galaxy with an HII classification, hosts an exceptional compact, isolated disk displaying minimal star formation activity. This rare phenomenon is persisting due to the ongoing interaction of the galaxy with its surrounding gaseous matter. This project aims to investigate the current state of UGC 8839's disk and its surroundings utilizing a comprehensive dataset consisting of optical, ultraviolet, infrared, and radio wave observations. The analysis of its optical and ultraviolet spectra reveals a relatively quiescent compact galaxy, characterized by its weak hydrogen emission and pronounced absorption features. The UV observations from GALEX show a distinct ring-like structure surrounding a smaller, central area with reduced intensity. The IR data from WISE and SPIRE reveal a larger disk extent in the far-IR band. The analysis of 21 cm radio waves from NASA's ALFALFA survey indicates the presence of massive, cold gas. The combined research suggests that a massive cloud of intergalactic matter is responsible for the peculiar central area of UGC 8839, comprising a smaller, central calix and a larger, far-IR disk. The study of this phenomenon offers an exceptional natural laboratory to study the interaction between galaxies and their surroundings.

For a minimally oriented quasiregular mapping that is nonconstant and comformally regular, we prove that the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set is less than or equal to one. Furthermore, if the mapping has a particular average behavior (on average, it acts like a biholomorphism) over a specific region with a particular characteristic (its boundary consists of polycircular domains), we demonstrate that the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set is less than one. Our findings build upon previous research of the second author and the first author's recent results.

Using the Empirical Model of the Atmosphere, a comprehensive analysis was conducted of the propagation of gravity waves in the Martian atmosphere, based on density data collected by four spacecraft: the Mars Global Surveyor, the Mars Odyssey, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and the Mars Science Laboratory. This study examines the spatial distribution and movement of these waves in the upper layers of the atmosphere, specifically between 80 and 300 km in altitude. Research demonstrates that, in accordance with theoretical expectations, the waves exhibit horizontal propagation. However, the observed vertical propagation is not consistently supported. The analysis also reveals that, in line with established convention, the waves exhibit increased amplitude in regions of stronger gravity, including the Jezero Crater and areas surrounding polar mesoscale features. The results show that the majority of the waves identified have a horizontal spacing of 200-1000 km and a vertical spacing of 5-10 km. The waves exhibited movement to lower latitudes, except in the southern hemisphere during the southern hemisphere's polar winter, when movement towards the north was observed. The findings from all investigated atmospheric levels match the established theory regarding the relationship between wave amplitude and pressure scale height. The analysis also reveals that, in the upper layers of the atmosphere, the waves exhibit increased amplitude in regions of stronger gravity, including the Jezero Crater and areas surrounding polar mesoscale features.

The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This analysis delves into the production of J/ψ mesons in Pb-Pb ultra-peripheral collisions, examining findings from the 2015-2018 data collection period during LHC Run 2. Specifically, it explores J/ψ forward production cross-sections in Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV, focusing on differential measurements with respect to rapidity, energy, and transverse momentum. In addition, it presents the mean $x_{\mathbf{\text{Pb}}}$-weighted $b_{\text{TPC}}$ lifetime of J/ψ mesons within the 0–10% most central collisions. Comparisons with the model predicting photon-induced J/ψ production using the (d/dx)LAMBDA photoproton cross-section from the H1 experiment are also included.

A novel sound visualization method is introduced, enabling the generation of acoustic effects that accurately correspond to visible patterns. This is achieved through the use of a data-driven approach, where a neural network creates a synthesis program responsive to image inputs. To facilitate the correlation of visual patterns with their underlying acoustic equivalents, a statistical framework is applied to identify and evaluate the inherent relationships between sound properties and perceived distortions. This analysis reveals how the preferred outcomes of unsupervised network training are influenced by local optima stemming from distinct visual-sound interpretations. To optimize performance, a supervised strategy is developed, leveraging pre-defined targets to train the network. The resulting system is capable of producing high-quality audio effects in sync with visual inputs, demonstrating the significance of acoustic feedback in shaping visual perceptions and enhancing the creativity of generative sound art experiments.

This study examines how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can be utilized for the acquisition of sequential temporal knowledge. Unlike traditional supervised learning methods, which require labeled data, this research explores a novel approach where a deep RNN can be trained in an unsupervised setting. By leveraging task-specific rewards as guidance, the network's sequential temporal knowledge is refined through trial-and-error experiences. This study showcases the ability of deep RNNs to extract meaningful temporal structures from high-dimensional input sequences, exemplified by tasks such as temporal credit assignment and predicting future event timings in uncertainty-rich scenarios.

Finding a balance between economic well-being and public health during a pandemic is crucial. By modeling the progression of infections and implementing non-pharmaceutical interventions among susceptible populations, our study investigates the optimal timing of interventions that minimize both health-related fatalities and economic losses. Initially, we establish a basic theoretical framework that can be applied to any pandemic scenario characterized by a nonlinear disease spread and a linear economic impact. One of the key findings from our framework is that the ideal policy involves a two-phase approach: an initial temporary pause in interventions, followed by a continuous implementation of some level of intervention. By employing a widely applicable model to the pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2, we demonstrate that the optimal policy is also applicable to real-world situations, even those with limited data availability. Our analytical approach reveals that the optimal policy is not only feasible but also reliable, making it useful for practical pandemic management.

This research introduces an innovative method to identify and rank data assets according to their influence on model predictions within a machine learning pipeline. To achieve this, we expanded the Shapley value framework, addressing its longstanding challenges related to computation and interpretation. Our method seamlessly integrates with existing model explanation tools, enabling users to make data asset selection decisions through informative insights. A demonstration case illustrates the practical application of our approach, while empirical evaluations using publicly available datasets and machine learning models replicate real-world troubleshooting scenarios, demonstrating its efficacy and cost-effectiveness.

This work explores various combinations of the aforementioned fields by
enumerating graphical models, analyzing tensor networks, and studying loop models.
Specifically, we delve into the asymptotic enumeration of random simple graphs,
random ratio matrices, and random ratio loops. To achieve this, we develop
mathematical frameworks that incorporate a new approach to degree-based
generating functions and precise estimates for the critical probability distribution
in zero-temperature quantum criticality. These models hold crucial significance as
they accurately represent the thermodynamic properties of quantum systems. Building
on established ideas, including past work and research on ratio schemes, our
approach provides significant insights into the underlying probability distributions.

This study presents an investigation of how high pressure affects the anomalous Hall effect in the triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn. Synchrotron X-ray diffraction and transport experiments were conducted to observe changes in crystal structure and electrical resistance under pressure. The results showed that increasing pressure beyond 1.5 GPa transforms the material's magnetic order, altering its 120-degree spin arrangement. This structural change triggered a significant increase in the material's anomalous Hall resistance, reversing its initial decline with pressure. Furthermore, an unusual magnetoelastic anomaly was detected in this material at pressures around 1.5 GPa, as indicated by spin reorientation magnetic transitions and an elastic constant anomaly. This anomaly is believed to result from competing exchange interactions and an inherent magnetorotational property in Mn$_3$Sn.

Research in relation extraction (RE) using deep neural networks (DNN) has garnered significant interest in recent years. An in-depth examination of the progress made in this area is necessary to establish a clear understanding of the advantages and drawbacks of DNN-based RE approaches. This paper provides an insightful analysis of the recent advancements in RE through a systematic review of studies in the field, focusing on classification methods and datasets employed. It also identifies prominent trends, key challenges, and future research directions in this area. Furthermore, it highlights the limitations of current evaluation methods used to assess the performance of supervised learning models.

This article delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Firstly, we establish the existence of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions for this problem. Next, we prove that the eigenvalues we've identified behave asymptotically like those of the Steklov problem in a hollow domain. Additionally, we demonstrate the interlacing property of eigenvalues when the parameter $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are varied. Lastly, we investigate the unbounded sequence of eigenvalues that arise as the parameter $\gamma$ becomes infinite.

We are given a complete hypergraph where the large edges have been removed, 
and we want to use the remaining vertices and remaining edges to estimate the 
original structure. This is known as the guided hypergraph reconstruction problem, 
and we can use a method called maximum likelihood estimation to solve it. We've 
developed a statistical model to analyze this problem and have found that 
as the number of vertices grows, the estimated solution gets closer to the 
original structure under certain conditions. Our experiments confirm the 
findings and provide further insight into this problem.

To advance automatic analysis of X-ray images, particularly in understanding abnormalities and ignoring irrelevant information, it is crucial to develop accurate annotations. However, producing such annotations is labor-intensive, hindering the progress in the field. Our proposed method leverages the advantages of both unenhanced X-ray images and three-dimensional chest computed tomography scans to create detailed annotations for abnormal regions on X-ray images. Since the visual aspects of X-ray images cannot be replicated through just spatial transformations, we employ a neural-based technique that combines the strengths of contrastive learning and image generation to effectively annotate abnormal regions. As there are limited training samples available, we also employ a data augmentation technique that incorporates information from the associated CT scan to produce high-quality synthetic training samples. Our method demonstrates exceptional performance on detecting and localizing abnormalities, particularly in lung lesions, and also demonstrates efficiency through an analysis of training time and spatial location precision.

Tight contact structures have become increasingly prominent due to their inherent rigidity. Given a tight contact 3-manifold, defining the Thurston norm is achievable and it possesses key properties, such as non-negativity and circular inequality. The Euler characteristic can be determined for any positive norm value. The set of possible Euler characteristic values for a fixed positive norm value can be any integer 0 to infinity, including jumps and discontinuities. The presence of singularities complicates things as it sometimes results in reduced characteristic values. The relationship between the Euler characteristic and the norm is not a linear or polynomial function.

Increasing control over the spatial orientation and timing of photon emissions is crucial in developing advanced solid-state light sources. We have identified a method to measure the anisotropy and unpolarized time-forward time-backward emission properties of microcavity lasers using entropy analysis. By studying the entropy of the system's density matrix, we can determine the amount of anisotropy, thus providing a comprehensive understanding of both properties. This method aligns with modern quantum information focus on unified treatment of unpolarized emission and emission directionality.

The meteoric rise of cryptocurrencies has its roots in their potential as a secure payment system. However, their adoption as a means of exchange is hindered by excessive transaction costs, primarily due to the reliance on blockchains. This study demonstrates, using a mathematical approach, that a consistent equilibrium exists with low transaction costs, achieved through the integration of off-chain payments. This results in fees being proportional to the value of the transaction, leading to significantly reduced costs.

For the KPZ equation, whose geometrically restricted version is defined on a closed interval, research has shown that low-level background noise can be interpreted as a weak perturbation of the KPZ equation. This noise has two distinct characteristics: it is gentle and highly probable. Building on this understanding, we introduce a new, more refined background noise that shares these two attributes. This background noise is based on the periodic inverse scattering of the ZS system and arises from the large-scale behavior of integrable non-coinciding two-component Bozlak's equation. To substantiate this, we establish a direct link between the probability distribution of this background noise and the probability distribution of rare events in the KPZ equation, as first proposed by Matsumoto and Sato. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our background noise is equitable in the sense of probability and probability density distributions.

MMS mission data provides valuable insights into the solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence. Analyzing data from both the Fast Plasma Instrument and the Spin Plane Double Probe, we discovered that the detectable footprint of this turbulence is heavily influenced by the solar wind's speed and magnetic field strength. Throughout most of the solar wind, the turbulence is highly anisotropic, characterized by scale sizes of $d_\lambda=f^{-1/3}(\vec{k}_\perp)^{-2/3}$, affecting both electron density and temperature. However, when the solar wind's density increases, the turbulence becomes more directional, involving electron temperature fluctuations on smaller scales. Two unusual solar wind streams are examined in detail. In the first, the solar wind's speed and density met specific criteria, revealing a distinct difference between electron density and temperature fluctuations via BiBi analysis. In the second, the solar wind's speed was notably higher, revealing a distinct difference between electron density and temperature fluctuations via the SpSp detection method. Our research indicates that temperature fluctuations are less active than density fluctuations by a factor of ~5. We also identify potential mechanisms for generating $E\times B$ vorticity in these turbulence patterns.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer X-rays. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show that, in practice, this modulation yields usable pulses within a few hundred attoseconds for X-rays in the range of 10-20 nm. Furthermore, this technique can be applied to existing facilities with minimal adjustments and is a crucial step towards generating single, ultra-short pulses in X-ray free electron lasers.

A method to estimate the direction and strength of a layered viscous shear flow by analyzing the variability of temperature within a database has been investigated. The method is based on an approximation, which we refer to as the physical optics model, that describes the variability in terms of a direction quasi-correlation function. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through its application to synthetic and real temperature data from various sources. The results show that the physical optics model accurately estimates the angle and intensity of the shear profile with a high level of precision, even in the presence of noisy data.

We've developed an unconventional method to quantify the unfair manipulation of voting districts by mimicking thermal behavior. By applying (pseudo-)thermal coefficients to electoral maps, we're able to identify signs of gerrymandering, such as unusual thermal conductivity or heat dispersal. These metrics have proven effective in assessing the problem across various case studies, making them easily calculable and applicable to real-world voting data, as demonstrated by our example based on North Carolina's 2011 congressional elections.

A novel flaw detection algorithm for patterned textiles is proposed, featuring an anisotropic direction-flaw identifier that leverages gradient-based orientation analysis and binarization. This comprehensive method comprises two primary stages: firstly, it employs Horizontal-Gradient Oriented Gradient (GHOG) to pinpoint the direction of flaws in desaturated image fragments; secondly, it utilizes low-rank decomposition combined with mixed-norm regularization to reconstruct flaw-containing fragments in the original image, thereby achieving accurate identification of flaws at the image level. Experimental outcomes confirm the efficacy of this algorithm, which outperforms existing flaw detection techniques while exhibiting greater robustness across diverse types of patterned textiles.

To enhance robotic visual navigation across complex and dynamic environments, this study presents a novel framework that integrates information-theoretic concepts with reinforcement learning. By formulating a target function that maximizes environmental discovery, the proposed method leverages mutual information as a metric for exploring unfamiliar areas. This study demonstrates the efficacy of its framework by adapting it to existing reinforcement learning techniques, specifically Q-learning and proximal policy optimization, and evaluates its performance on two comprehensive datasets, Mean-averaged discrepancy and ALFRED. The results indicate that the proposed method accelerates learning and boosts performance compared to traditional reinforcement learning, showcasing its potential for robust visual navigation in intricate environments.

Research indicates that emissions of gravitational waves by near-Extreme Black Holes can lead to a decrease in their mass through the Bondi process, causing their mass to diminish at a constant rate when in a state of Bondi equilibrium.  Focusing on Black Holes spanning a range of charges and angular momenta, this study aims to determine a general upper limit on the rate of mass reduction associated with Bondi emissions.  It is assumed that the emitter is non-rotating, which simplifies calculations and enables a comprehensive analysis of the emission spectrum.  The study utilizes a standard approach to describe the continuum emission, applying the Teitelboim-Tafel-Bondi formalism to express the emission spectrum in terms of the Bondi mass, radiation rate, and energy.  Considering that the emitter is in a state of Bondi equilibrium, its mass and radiation rate are closely related, which in turn enables a connection between the emission intensity and the rate of mass reduction.  The intensity of the radiation is measured by the rate of photon energy per unit solid angle, which is shown to be a function of the mass reduction rate, radiation rate, and Bondi energy, adjusted for observational considerations.  Observations of a Boni equilibrium Black Hole with a mass of approximately 15 solar masses would require a significant reduction in mass of about $10^{-6} \dot{M}_{\odot}/(1 \,{\rm s})$, which could be detected using

We examine the formation of primordial supersymmetries through the collision of left-over first-star remnants in dense nuclear clusters at the heart of massive early galaxies. Our research indicates that these early star clusters experienced a high level of star formation activity and are now enveloped by a vast amount of dark matter. We project that heavy primordial supersymmetries will form in the clusters' centers and remain stable for an extended period. Our predictions show that future gravitational wave detectors like LISA will have the capability to detect the low-frequency gravitational waves produced by these supersymmetry breakages, with detection rates ranging from a few hundred to tens of thousands per year. These early star cluster origins can be differentiated from more conventional black hole sources using specific characteristics at low frequencies or by employing multiple detection methods.

In the context of smart cities, the concept of Power Distribution Grids intelligence offers enhanced efficiency and performance. However, the current paper shifts its focus to the challenges of incident identification, which logistically demands hands-on field work to pinpoint problems. To this end, this study introduces a data-driven approach that locates incidents based on real-time meter readings sent back to the Substation, which are then analyzed by a computer algorithm to detect anomalies and pinpoint their source. To test the validity of this proposed method, simulations were run using artificial data generated to resemble real-world PDG meter readings, which were then used to demonstrate the efficacy of this proposed technique.

Our study focuses on examining the radiative and electromagnetic decays of the $X(3872)\pi\gamma$ and involve determining the X(3872) form factor. To achieve this, we employed two methods: 

  The first used a Lagrangian description to calculate the form factor, accounting for the X(3872) composition under quark and resonance matter. 
  The second method involved a phenomenological approach using the X(3872) decay to J/psi pi pi, and applicable corrections for radiative decay to J/psi pi gamma. 

Our findings from the two methods show notable discrepancies in the X(3872) form factor, particularly evident at lower Q^2 values. 
The differences between the two approaches can be attributed to potential issues in the X(3872) composition, identified in our investigations. 
The X(3872) is likely a tetraquark or an excited hadronic state, and our results are comparable to both scenarios. 
The X(3872) width to radiation and pi pi radiation decays were also derived and are inclusive of non-resonant contributions. 
The X(3872) width to radiation decay lies within experimental limits, and our results for the pi pi radiation decay are consistent with current data. 
Our study offers new areas for experimental investigation and fresh perspectives on the X(3872) composition.

We provide a comprehensive description of smooth quadrics within the context of bounded symmetric domains, offering categorical representations of symplectic and arithmetic triads in the process. This description enables the classification of quadrics up to categorial equivalence, allowing us to derive insights into their geometric and arithmetic characteristics in the course of proof.

Text-based games provide a platform to analyze and improve virtual agents' ability to understand natural language by generating actions based on text inputs. However, current text-based games are restricted by their reliance on slow recursive actions, such as dynamic character movements, which hinder their scalability. Our research introduces TextWorldExpress, an optimized framework that leverages vector operations to enhance performance, allowing for over one million steps per second, an eight-fold improvement over existing designs. By developing this efficient framework, we conducted extensive experiments to examine the impact of various game properties and computed optimal policies using both online and offline training methods, utilizing both simple and complex game examples. Our study demonstrates the potential for high-speed text-based games to facilitate online learning and also identifies limitations and challenges that need to be addressed.

We develop an approach to define A-symmetries spatially, despite underlying flaws in the construction, which persists even through perturbative corrections. This methodology is exemplified in protecting Topological Insulators' properties and ensuring momentum stability within gapped systems.

Consider a constant p greater than or equal to 1. In this study, we will explore properties of p-harmonic functions within angular sectors in two-dimensional space, specifically those sectors where p is greater than or equal to 2π. A p-harmonic function is defined as the solution to the equation ∆_p u = 0 in a given domain Ω, where p is a constant, and this equation is satisfied throughout a larger region that includes Ω as its interior. Previous researchers have shown that p-harmonic functions have mean value properties in certain domains such as half-spaces and domains bounded by cones. Our research will demonstrate that these p-harmonic functions also possess mean value properties in sectors with a constant opening angle, and that these mean value properties are valid for any value of p greater than or equal to 1. Additionally, our research will show that the distance of a given point u from a ball is proportional to the mean value of the function φ over the boundary of the ball, where φ is a given p-harmonic function, and this result is true for small enough radii R. Our research will also demonstrate that the distance of a given point u from a ball is proportional to the mean value of the function φ over the boundary of the ball, where φ is a given p-harmonic function, and this result is true for large enough radii R when 1 < p < 2.

Significant wind and wave conditions prevalent in extreme marine environments have
resultant effects on coastal erosion, shoreline destruction, and oil field equipment
damage. These severe weather events also have a profound impact on coastal communities,
resulting in numerous accidents and fatalities. To analyze these critical phenomena,
researchers utilize spatial analysis and multivariate statistical models, focusing on the
distribution of extreme weather event frequencies across different locations. This
paper introduces a novel spatial model for analyzing multivariate extreme weather data,
outlining a new approach to understanding the relationship between weather event intensities
and geographic locations. This novel multivariate spatial model incorporates the unique
characteristics of extreme marine weather distributions, incorporating the concepts of
exchangeability and stochastic development. By employing hierarchical modeling and
Bayesian inference, researchers can estimate the parameters of this novel model,
simultaneously testing hypotheses regarding the dependence of weather event intensities
on location. To illustrate the efficacy of this novel spatial model, researchers applied
it to a real-world dataset of wind and wave measurement data collected from Bukira Island
off the coast of Liberia.

This article investigates the infiniteness of trigonometric functions and hypergeometric functions defined over complex numbers, with coefficients based on rational numbers or prime numbers, in relation to their analogs defined over number fields. Key arguments involve the use of transcendence measures such as the logarithm and exponential functions, as well as the properties of specific number theoretic functions like the Riemann zeta function and the Dirichlet L-functions. By integrating these concepts, we establish the infiniteness of various functions, including elliptic functions, heat kernel functions, and hypergeometric functions, within the context of complex numbers and number fields.

A rapidly expanding field known as collaborative robotics focuses on enabling robots to operate alongside humans in a shared workspace. This research centers on developing robots capable of working alongside humans in a shared environment, encompassing tasks such as food preparation and emergency response, which necessitate the robots' ability to follow human instructions and adapt to unfamiliar objects and situations. This requires the creation of robots that can seamlessly integrate human-given instructions and adapt to unfamiliar objects and situations. While current collaborative robotics platforms typically utilize ego-centric human motion capture for tracking, this technology can be unreliable in everyday settings due to potential malfunctions and restrictions on wearable devices. Consequently, we implement a novel and robust method for tracking based on optical flow that leverages deep learning, aiming to provide high-quality input-data for our proposed learning-based system. This system enables the robots to accurately follow scaled-down representations of human-directed movements, encompassing a range of gestures, such as pointing, grabbing, and rotating, without requiring prior knowledge of robot dynamics or other robots. To ensure effective learning, we employ a novel method for providing feedback to the robots, which aligns well with a theoretical framework for learning based on structured interactions between humans and robots. Through experiments using a sophisticated simulation environment and real-world testing, we demonstrate that our approach can successfully transfer learning from a simulated to a real-world setting, facilitating more efficient and robust adaptation to new objects and situations.

In experiments at the Large Hadron Collider, detecting Higgs boson pairs in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ decay faces significant challenges due to overwhelming background interference. This background can be minimized using event selection that relies on enhanced matrix element information about the proton-proton collision. Here, we explore potential gains in observing Higgs boson pair events of this type when incorporating matrix element-based criteria into the event identification process. To achieve this, we create fast and efficient tools for matrix element computation, allowing for rapid event categorization. This process evaluates the relevance of each event based on whether its matrix element significantly exceeds that of standard model predictions, thus identifying Higgs boson pair candidates with enhanced accuracy. Additionally, we investigate whether incorporating off-shell Higgs boson corrections and triple Higgs boson coupling into the matrix element can improve Higgs boson pair detection.

Turntables 3D objects, commonly found in CAD models, are exactly that - three-dimensional objects designed to rotate in various ways. They're not programmed to stop spinning at specific angles; instead, their 3D shape determines when a suitable pose is reached. Researchers have now found that, in most cases, a turntable's 3D layout can be figured out just by observing its rotational views - without needing prior knowledge. This is remarkable, given that predicting a 3D shape from rotational images is known to be an even harder problem, an achievement that was previously thought to be more advanced. To study this, a dataset of 32 turntables, along with around 15,000 images, was created by researchers and tested several approaches on this new challenge. In the end, a model called 'ThreeDUNsup' was developed to determine a turntable's 3D layout just by observing its rotational views - all without needing prior knowledge. This model uses a self-attention device and learned layout representations, and was found to consistently and accurately determine a turntable's 3D layout. This breakthrough has far-reaching implications, given the abundance of turntable models available. For instance, identifying a car's 3D layout just by looking at its rotating wheels could greatly simplify self-driving technology. Or, determining a character's 3D layout from viewing angles in 3D could greatly improve video games and animation.

Misinformation dissemination through social media has been a major public health concern, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. To combat this issue, governments and health organizations have partnered with technology companies to counteract the spread of false information about coronavirus and vaccines. Addressing this challenge, our study aims to develop effective strategies for automated systems to detect acceptance or rejection of misinformation related to COVID-19 vaccines posted on Twitter. We have compiled a unique dataset consisting of dialogues on Twitter, encompassing real-world conversations about vaccine misinformation. This dataset is used to conduct multiple experiments using various machine learning algorithms, followed by an analysis of the results to define key performance metrics. Building upon these findings, our research proposes two novel algorithms: the Dialogues-Based Acceptance/Rejection Identification (DARI) algorithm and its enhanced version, DARI-Pro. These algorithms outperform existing automated systems, setting them apart with their ability to accurately determine both the speaker's perspective and the response's persuasive intention towards the speaker's perspective. Our research contributes to the development of automated systems capable of detecting acceptance or rejection of misinformation and promotes the creation of persuasive responses to counteract the spread of false information on Twitter.

A key feature of high-field laser physics is the rapid and precise control of light, enabling the creation and manipulation of extreme ultraviolet pulses on an isolated timescale (several quadrillionths of a second). These pulses, known as single-quantum pulses, can be generated through unique laser patterns that prevent overlapping, such as using difference-frequency generation or optical solitonic behavior. Our study focuses on an alternative and robust approach to coherent pulse manipulation using a simple yet effective arrangement of few-cycle IR pulses and their second harmonic, producing isolated XUV pulses in a predictable and reliable manner. This straightforward mechanism, in addition to easily modifiable pulse manipulation capabilities, makes it an ideal choice for generating single-quantum pulses and exploring extreme ultraviolet pulse coherences in experiments based on interferometry and attophysics.

Recent discoveries of additional companions to the Algol star system in 2019 and 2020 have been reported, which were found using photometric monitoring and data from various surveys.  These new findings were found by examining data that had not been published previously.  Upon conducting a more detailed analysis of the system's light, it was determined that the previously reported companions were actually explained by changes associated with Algol's established orbital cycle, and did not require an additional companion to account for.  Specifically, it was found that the system's light variation could be described using a combination of linear and quadratic terms, eliminating the need for any irregular fluctuations.  Furthermore, it was found that the system's light varies in a way that is influenced by Algol's established orbital cycle, but does not exhibit the type of variations that would be expected if there were additional companions.

This research investigates the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a focus on initial conditions surrounding a compact, convex obstacle in three-dimensional space. Specifically, we demonstrate that any given exponential initial condition leading to explosive solutions is encompassed by a linearly weighted $H^{1}_{\infty}$-modulo-compactness class of initial conditions, leading to explosive outcomes.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further advancements in further research are still required due to issues related to precision, stability, and dimensionality. The primary obstacle is the need to begin with dense grid points from the start. In this study, we introduce a vertex creation method called Residual Adaptive Vertex creation by binning with Nearby points, or RANG, that uses a straightforward yet highly effective approach to create a variable density grid on the fly during the training process based on the discrepancies between the continuous and discrete solutions. This method enhances the accuracy and efficiency of physics-informed neural networks, allowing it to be applied to a broader range of problems, including nonlinear and differential equations with varying dimensions and distances. Additionally, we compared RANG with the current top-rated vertex creation method, revealing that it yields results that are both precise and consistently better, particularly in challenging scenarios. The code for this study is made accessible through a link to a GitHub repository.

This study examines the behavior of a pseudo-static random number generator based on ferroelectric FETs, which suffers from setbacks due to increased overlap capacitance and variable channel resistance. A mathematical model is developed to analyze the capacitive effects on transistor performance, revealing that these interactions can produce oscillating gate voltages with varying frequency and amplitude depending on the transistor characteristics. Furthermore, we investigate how these capacitive interactions impact the transistor's current response, which in this multi-domain FeFET, corresponds to varying current levels at the output of the generator due to domain wall movements. Additionally, we discuss how these capacitive phenomena can produce additional statistics, known as deleterious capacitance, which can cause parts of the output spectrum to be obscured. To overcome this issue, we propose a solution that involves utilizing a series resistor in the gate feedline to mitigate the capacitive effects, which, however, introduces an upper limit on which frequency can be generated.

The increasing complexity of freight system operations necessitates comprehensive knowledge of the interdependencies among freight system components to avoid and mitigate potential disruptions. This research develops a freight system dependency graph based on case studies of 12 freight providers and their networks. It also identifies common failure patterns across these providers, contributing to an understanding of freight system vulnerability. This research aims to facilitate identification and classification of freight system weaknesses, as well as help freight providers strengthen their systems to reduce their vulnerability to disruptions.

For analyzing the dynamical behavior of matter in physical systems, researchers employ the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation, which can be modified to include random noise and applied to various applications such as superfluids and water wave equations. Introducing unique, salt-and-pepper-type noise into this equation allows researchers to study the irreducibility of resulting stochastic differential equations, which has important implications in determining a process's distinctness and understanding its ability to be reduced to lower-dimensional systems. Additionally, calculating the irreducibility rate and establishing the $L^2$-norm convergence of trajectories in terms of initial data is also crucial in characterizing a process's uniqueness and understanding its ability to be followed by lower-dimensional systems. Applying this theory to the study of both deterministic and stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations, researchers find that the presence of random noise helps to establish the uniqueness of trajectories and the irreducibility of resulting stochastic equations, which is crucial in understanding a system's dynamical behavior in the presence of random disturbances.

Let $G$ be a finite nilpotent group, and let $\phi(G)$ represent the smallest degree of a polynomial whose roots comprise all elements of $G$ when evaluated. Our analysis determines upper limits for $\phi(G)$ based on the prime factors of $G$s nilpotency class.

I'm primarily involved with the MOE, a key component of the FAIR experiment, where I'm responsible for detecting hyperons produced in beam-target collisions. This experience piqued my interest in a proposed Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiment that would utilize a similar range of detecting technologies. This experiment would serve two purposes: Firstly, it would examine non-relativistic hadron interactions at very low energies, which are currently not well-understood. Secondly, it would investigate cosmic radiation phenomena with significant advantages over existing methods. My proposal outlines the experimental setup, detector technologies, and necessary infrastructure required for this project.

Deep learning models have been widely used for image classification, with successful results reported with various modifications. Nonetheless, the application of these models to oriented images has proven challenging, as existing models fail to account for the rotational degree. In this paper, we introduce the Orientation Convolutive Network (OCN), a novel network design that incorporates the rotational degree, thereby enabling effective classification of oriented images. In our experiments, OCN demonstrated superior performance compared to conventional networks and a previously proposed Special Oriented Network.

This study seeks to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of point cloud processing tasks, such as classification and segmentation. To achieve this, we thoroughly examine various design elements of graph convolutional networks, including the construction of graph models, aggregation methods, and fusion operations. Our investigation involves comparing different strategies for classification and segmentation tasks, using the MESSYGF library to replicate the experiments and gather notable results, which highlight the significance of appropriate graph construction and aggregation methods for point cloud processing.

A new kind of attack on deep learning models has emerged, where it is possible for malicious neural networks to deceive users into performing desired actions through subtle changes, regardless of the model architecture or processing device. One approach, known as the backdoor attack, involves training a robust neural network to exhibit one behavior when functioning normally, and a different behavior when triggered by specific input, often incorporated during training. Most existing backdoor attacks and defensive strategies rely on hardware-based unique identifiers, such as CPU IDs or GPU addresses, to construct backdoors, which are embedded in the model during training and reliant on specific hardware configurations. However, this can make it difficult to create models that work across multiple platforms or need to be deployed on new hardware setups. A new attack method, known as HOSTA, allows malicious neural networks to develop backdoors tied to specific software or system features, rather than relying on unique hardware identifiers. These features often involve user behavior, such as specific input data, which can be utilized to construct backdoors. HOSTA also enables multiple backdoors to be tied to distinct features, allowing a highly adaptable and resource-efficient attack, particularly when compared to existing attacks using neural bandits or poison attacks. To evaluate the effectiveness of HOSTA, we tested two practical scenarios, one involving image nets and another with language models, demonstrating the difficulty of detecting this type of attack using current defensive methods.

We have enhanced the functionality of the Magellan-IMACS-ROSIE (MagIC) instrument with an integral field module (IFM). This module allows the e2d CCD detector to capture 20 separate 0.256 arcsecond x 50.0 arcminute spectra, arranged in a 2.5 x 20 format, across a 50 arcminute field of view. 
By integrating the IFM with MagIC, which features a 4.5 arcsecond x 50.0 arcminute spatial resolution and 1350 recollection ability, the system is now capable of simultaneously observing up to 20 individual galaxies in a single 50 arcminute field of view. 
This integrated system, MagIC-IFM, was officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially officially implemented in April 2021 and was used to gather data for a study focusing on the evolution of a specific class of galaxies called quasars. 
This study, which aimed to determine the rate at which these galaxies produce new material and release energy, utilized the instrument's ability to analyze multiple objects in a single observation. 
In doing so, the team was able to identify a relationship between a galaxies mass and the rate at which it releases energy, as well as the rate at which it produces new material.
