A compelling case can be made that the substantial time requirement of machine learning, 
along with its labor-intensive preparation phase, serves as a significant barrier, 
exerting a considerable influence on users.  This research delves into the possibilities of 
utilizing a compiler to automate the training and setup of models, aiming to reduce 
setups time and associated costs.  Investigating the prospects of compiling ML models, 
we identified key challenges in this area of study.  Through our experimental evaluation, 
we demonstrated that compiling ML models poses a considerable computational burden on 
resource-constrained devices, such as a Raspberry Pi.  While compiling ML models may not 
be feasible from a practical standpoint, our study contributes to the growing body of 
research focused on employing compilers to streamline machine learning setup, offering users 
faster and more efficient experiences.

The investigation of dark matter directly offers a pioneering way to
understand its nature, albeit challenging due to the lack of a definitive
detection method. Typically, researchers rely on particle physics detectors to
capture evidence, but a novel study suggests utilizing nuclear reactors to
produce sub-GeV dark matter candidates. When interacting with matter, these
particles would result in the breaking of nuclei and the emission of electrons
or X-rays. To correlate the generated electrons with their primary sources,
researchers can employ time-projection chamber detectors, which incorporate
thin, high-Z materials targeting the production of electrons through nuclear
decay. By amplifying the sensitivity to detect dark matter, this method could
potentially reveal the properties of sub-GeV dark matter particles previously
eluded scientists. A 100 kg equivalent-mass detector located 10 meters away
from a high-power nuclear reactor and with a 4-year run time, could potentially
determine the cross-section value with a confidence level of 5 sigma for
dark matter masses below 1 GeV, with this value rising to 10 sigma for masses
less than 200 MeV. Furthermore, studying sub-GeV dark matter through nuclear
reactions not only offers a distinctive way to detect this type of matter, but
it also offers the possibility to investigate various non-perturbative dark
matter theories, thereby expanding scientific research in this field.

This paper proposes a method to achieve stable, symmetric transmission of quantum information for two discrete point dips in the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model. It's shown that contrasting entanglement dynamics between two distinct initial states results in either complete entanglement of the qubit and the cavity mode or maintenance of nonentangled qubits, respectively. Furthermore, the system's ability to transmit information reliably is linked to a combination of classical and quantum correlations between the cavity mode and the qubit. Two applications of this model are explored: one results in stable, symmetric point dips that support quantum information transmission, and the other yields stable, asymmetric dip structures without supporting information transmission. It's demonstrated that adjusting the qubit frequency enables control over the entanglement degree of the cavity mode, while maintaining nonentangled qubits. Finally, two discrete point dips in the system's emission spectra are identified, each with distinct entanglement properties.

Measuring inter-beat intervals provides insight into cardiovascular function but current methods using deep learning have shown less than desirable accuracy. We propose a new approach that combines ResNet and DenseNet architectures, referred to as Tiramisu Model, for predicting inter-beat intervals from electrocardiogram signals. Our model can function as both a lead feature extractor or a standalone model and demonstrates high efficiency and accuracy, outperforming existing deep learning methods and achieving an average error rate of 3.63% with a processing speed of 0.044 ms per prediction.

This study examines deviations in an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle's behavior, which is influenced by multiple swimming robots, to better understand their collective movement. A modification is made to the particle's equation to account for the robots' nonlinear response, causing their movement to diverge from the particle's trajectory. To resolve these discrepancies, the researchers reworked the equation using variational techniques, which resulted in a new, simpler expression that aligns with the original particle dynamics when there are no swimming robots. To test the effectiveness of the new approach, the researchers conducted a series of simulations, which revealed that the corrected equation accurately describes the collective movement of the robots, particularly at lower swimming speeds. Additionally, the researchers discovered that the corrected equation can also be applied to a broader class of active particle models.

In everyday life, people use various forms of multiview visual recognition to navigate spaces and interact with others. Current models, however, struggle to process multiple views effectively. To bridge this gap, we've created HUMBI, a massive multiview dataset featuring 54,322 unique videos and 18,780 accompanying images. Capturing a range of gestures, the dataset includes 11 distinct categories with over 5,000 labeled segments per class. To demonstrate the utility of HUMBI, we've developed six benchmark tasks and conducted an extensive evaluation of existing models. The dataset and corresponding benchmark challenges can be found at https://humbi.github.io/.

This research investigates the possibility of using neural task representations as a form of weak supervision that enables model-independent cross-lingual transfer in NLP tasks. We propose a novel method, $f$, that maps sentence representations to task representations, and can be trained on data translated from any language. The key characteristic of our proposed method is that it can be applied across all languages, including those with limited data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully achieving state-of-the-art results on NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis and question-answering across a variety of languages, including languages that have never been trained on before. You can find the code to reproduce our results at: https://github.com/matir/neural-task-representations.

A key video super-resolution technique, VSR, has been widely recognized for its ability to restore high-resolution images from low-resolution video inputs, leveraging temporal information to generate sharper results. VSR techniques have demonstrated significant performance gains with the integration of advanced network architectures and temporal propagation methods. Our proposal, BasicVSR++, builds upon the BasicVSR model, initially presented in 2020, by refining its propagation and alignment components to produce superior VSR outcomes. In tests using the top-ranked evaluation tool, NTIRE, our model achieved outstanding performance, claiming the top spot in the VSR category for RGB images and ranking second only to a more complex model, VQSR, in the VSR (TCN) category.

In real-world scenarios, training agents to make sequential decisions in various situations is common, with multiple interconnected tasks often being encountered. Our study investigates how the interaction between tasks affects their resolution and demonstrates that co-training agents separately for each task, as is standard in multi-task reinforcement learning, can lead to detrimental effects when executed sequentially. This happens because the system's inability to isolate task responses causes interference that worsens over time. To address this, we propose a modular system that isolates task responses and reduces the impact of cross-talk between them. This method enhances learning efficiency and effectiveness across all tasks. Empirical validations were conducted using both synthetic and genuine data sets.

Working in an optimal manner, an ideal thermal machine should achieve the highest possible efficiency in any given situation. For a conventional Carnot engine, this optimum efficiency is reached when the control mechanism has access to the system's internal temperatures and pressures, resulting in the highest efficiency for a given set of thermal temperatures. This paper examines the performance of a Carnot engine when the control mechanism has limited access to the system's properties, specifically the final internal temperature. Under these circumstances, the optimum efficiency is attained when the control mechanism has precise knowledge of the system's average internal temperature. This result also holds true for other thermal processes and can be extended to situations involving an arbitrary number of thermal baths.

This research proposes a comprehensive framework to evaluate the impact of hurricanes and storm surges on the energy sector. To achieve this, three interconnected modules are developed: (1) a database driver to gather energy installation data, (2) a hazard simulator to model hurricanes and storm surges with varying intensities, and (3) a calculative core to measure energy installation losses. Each module is designed to be adaptable, allowing for easy integration of new data sources and computational methods. To facilitate flexible research directions, the framework's components can be modified at different levels: query formation, data extraction, algorithm definition, or model specification. To demonstrate its functionality, two case studies are conducted using historical hurricane events in the United States. The first analysis examines the total losses due to hurricanes in Florida, while the second explores the relative economic impact of storm surges on energy installations in New York and Florida. The results from these scenarios indicate that storm surges can significantly impair energy installations, and understanding their effects is essential to informing policy decisions.

In this study, we prove an extension of the three spheres theorem for monogenic functions under Clifford analysis framework. Specifically, given a monogenic function defined within a bounded domain V in a R^n+1 space, we demonstrate that it can be expressed as a sum of three unique polynomials, each confined to a distinct sphere centered on the origin. These spheres lie within V and have radii determined by the function's growth rate in three-dimensional spaces. This finding validates the original three spheres theorem for harmonic functions and establishes analogous results for functions governed by the Dirac and Kahananukko operators under specific conditions.

Approachability of entropy is highly dependent on the choice of sequences, such as those generated by the Dyck system, which does not adhere to this criterion. Investigating the motivator for developing approachability is essential. This paper compares ergodic measures of the Dyck system with those of the heterochaos baker map, a system that exhibits non-approachability of entropy. The study reveals that both systems have minimal and maximal entropy ground states, consisting of unique ergodic measures that cannot be split. These measures display the same ordinal and exhibit a 50% division ratio. However, the natural distribution associated with approachability fails in the Dyck system, whereas it exists in the heterochaos system. The failure of approachability in the Dyck system is attributed to the absence of local stability in its natural distribution, whereas the natural distribution of the heterochaos system shows both internal and external stability.

Beyond the standard model, the enhanced scalar sectors in alternative theories have the potential to be discovered at future colliders, with several paths to detection possible, including the observation of near-threshold production, resonance masses shifting, and light scalar masses, all of which offer groundbreaking opportunities for precision physics and accurate measurements of additional scalar masses. Additionally, the enhanced scalar sectors may interact differently with matter, influencing quantities such as lepton universality and flavor-changing neutral currents, making them pivotal areas of study, particularly at lepton colliders where low-background operations and abundant $W$ boson production provide favorable conditions.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as a quasi-periodic model for time-series prediction. However, the model's implicit quasi-periodic structure is not directed towards predicting speech features, leading to subpar pitch control. We introduce filter banks with explicit pitch-based preferences to refine the model's quasi-periodic structure, resulting in a more effective generative model for raw waveform synthesis. Experimental evaluations using the LJSpeech-1 dataset demonstrate that QPNet produces higher quality speech features compared to WN and prior methods, while also offering more flexible speech length and pitch control options.

In the era of collaborative filtering, where privacy and data sensitivity pose significant issues, the goal is to create personalized recommendations that respect users' individuality. This study investigates cooperative filtering, an innovative approach that leverages data from multiple sources anonymously to create comprehensive and transparent recommendations. The proposed biclustering method employs objective functions like squared loss and robust l1-norm to develop user and item profiling to maximise prediction accuracy. The objective of this research is to provide an extensive examination of cooperative filtering's underlying assumptions and provide insights into its effectiveness in addressing key challenges associated with the development of recommendation systems.

The optimal strategy for mastering stellar activity correction while searching for Earth-like planets via precision radial velocity monitoring is the focus of this study. We investigated the spectral features most sensitive to magnetic activity in a sample of actively rotating solar analogues by using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and then examined their potential utility as activity indicators. Compared to the established mesospheric stratospheric potassium line at 5270 nm, we found that a previously unidentified Fe I feature at 6301.5 nm is approximately ten times more responsive to solar activity. However, despite being impacted by temperature in the solar photosphere, it is largely unaffected by activity. Furthermore, we identified another important iron line at 6302.5 nm that is also heavily affected by solar activity. We also discovered that a previously overlooked water vapor line at 7780 nm is approximately ten times more sensitive to solar activity than the well-known Na I line at 5893 nm. Moreover, its formation is unrelated to temperature in the solar photosphere. We further refined the sensitivity of radial velocity to magnetic activity in the solar lines by correcting for temperature effects using a detailed model and a database of ionisation coefficients, and we updated the empirical relations for various spectral features.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal electrodes in tunneling spectroscopy with high-resistance electrodes in a sample with topological superconducting properties. The increased thermal fluctuations associated with these high-resistance electrodes will likely generate characteristic broadening in the tunneling conductance curve, which can be attributed to ohmic damping. The effect of this broadening should be more pronounced for scenarios involving Majorana modes as they are more sensitive to the density of states. We have found that the ratio of this broadening to the conductance peak's amplitude could serve as a reliable indicator of Majorana modes, and this indicator is notably less sensitive to noise that may arise from other sources.

M. Kapranov introduced the concept of shadows as a type of infinite-dimensional cluster algebraic structure, with morphism relations resembling those of quantum groups. Building on the work of B. Keller and the first author, this paper demonstrates that the category of shadows can be reinterpreted as a bicategory of rational fraction lattice paths, with transitions corresponding to flip moves. This results in a direct comparison with dendriform algebras, in addition to proving earlier conjectures of the first author and M. Umback.

Existing image enhancement techniques are limited in their ability to transfer styles from one image to another, particularly when it comes to correcting over-compressed images. A new, universal algorithm is introduced in this study that enables achieving various tones in images through a multi-scale, low-rank model, and demonstrates the ability to extract styles from picture pairs. The research also proves that a specific model, Low-Rank + Sparse Members, is capable of performing forward and reverse tone mapping. The authors evaluate the performance of their model on a vast dataset of 15 million images and show that it surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both forward and reverse tone mapping tasks.

This technical report outlines the rules and regulations of the AQTC Contest held during the 2022 Computer Vision Pattern Recognition conferences, detailing the objectives, evaluation criteria, and methodology of the contest. 

The report begins by explaining the purpose of the contest. To ensure fair assessment, we provide an objective evaluation protocol. Next, we outline the contest's technical requirements, including data preprocessing, model architecture, training, and inference protocols. We also define the evaluation metrics. The report concludes by summarizing the contest's rules and specifying the deadline for submission.

Field measurements reveal a unique pattern in snowfall, where larger particles accumulate at ground level, adhering to smaller particles, resulting in a highly selective deposition process. Understanding this process is crucial to clarifying observations of preferential selection in atmospheric turbulence, where particles of different densities and sizes exhibit unnatural correlations. We propose that gravitational attraction between particles is the primary driver of preferential selection, suggesting that larger particles preferentially stick to smaller particles, resulting in the observed density-dependent correlations. To validate our theory, we examine density and size preferences in detailed numerical simulations, and our results demonstrate a strong correlation with field measurements, validating the role of gravitational attraction in preferential selection.

Artificial intelligence methods like reinforcement learning can struggle with Robo-Taxi problems due to noisy rewards and uncertain state observations.  By utilizing the active inference framework, we propose an innovative solution that doesn't rely on global rewards or a full knowledge of the state space.  This approach develops a more in-depth understanding of the world by gathering local insights through exploratory movements.  Theoretical foundations and empirical evidence support the idea that more thorough explorations lead to greater certainty in the world map.  Empirical tests with a mobile robot demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in constructing a detailed environment and recovering from initial misinformation.

In experimental facilities, a sparse tape with picosecond resolution offers high-energy particle detection capabilities, requiring significant computational power for data processing. However, due to the low frequency of occurrences, the data is often dominated by vast amounts of zero values, leading to inefficient computational resource utilization. To address this issue, our research focuses on compressing three-dimensional sparse data into two-dimensional data while maintaining accuracy through a dual convolutional autoencoder structure. By replacing traditional fully connected layers with convolutional layers in both the encoder and decoder, we have optimized the autoencoder model for the sparse data format. Furthermore, we incorporated a dual convolutional structure in the encoder to divide the data into spatial and temporal features. Our experimental results demonstrate that the optimized autoencoder model achieves high compression ratios with minimal reconstruction error.

Building on previous work, the Finzi gravity model has been further developed by incorporating the effects of galactic clusters on dark matter distribution. This theoretical framework aims to reconcile the varying radial profiles observed in galactic clusters. This work employs the Finzi gravity model to analyze the dark matter distribution of galactic clusters using the Navarro-Frenk-White and Einasto models. To verify the model's predictions, a statistical test was conducted to compare the resulting radial profiles with observed data on 13 galactic clusters. The outcome indicates that neither the Navarro-Frenk-White nor Einasto models can accurately reproduce the radial profiles of all galactic clusters, as evident from the statistical errors obtained. Nonetheless, the analysis shows that the real-space slopes of the Einasto model match the predictions of the Finzi gravity model more accurately than those of the NFW model.

A type of geometric hypergraph is one where the intersections of its components resemble geometric shapes. This encompasses a range of applications, from the study of interconnected components in images to the investigation of certain types of networks. This paper explores a particular class of geometric hypergraphs linked to a problem originating from Tardos and Shor's study of a game. We identify challenges in fully resolving the problem and propose a related issue concerning the maximum number of 3-element subsets with a specific property within a set of n integers. We refer to this as the k-GEQ3 problem. Our proposals for addressing this issue include a upper bound based on a general approach for such problems and improved but still limited estimates derived from examining the specific structure of the k-GEQ3 problem.

The properties of discrete transition states and their relative properties are largely understood through the concept of the nuclear structure's symmetry, however the relationship becomes complex when dealing with continuum states as the nuclear structure's symmetry no longer directly applies. Research has shown that certain $\alpha$-cluster states in light nuclei exhibit symmetry, but computational methods such as the Generator Coordinate Method and the Resonating Group Method fail to generate these states directly, instead relying on the reaction cross-section to infer them, which is often subject to error. A new method has been proposed to directly generate symmetric $\alpha$-cluster states through the solution of the coupled-reaction matrix equations, which has been successful in the $^{6}$Li+$^{51}$V system. The method has demonstrated the ability to produce a narrow resonance below the particle threshold, consisting of an $S$-wave component with near-symmetric properties, along with an $D$-wave component that diverges at the threshold. The method has shown potential for widespread application across various nuclear reactions.

A previously (2019) described snake-like robot has been enhanced to mimic the behavior of a certain species of eel found in the Pacific Ocean. This updated bot can climb vertical surfaces with the assistance of a suction-based technique that doesn't require suction pumps; instead, it utilizes a controlled flow of water to create a vacuum effect. Furthermore, we've derived a mathematical model to illustrate the forces at play during this climbing method and demonstrated that the bot's movement is influenced by the flow rate of water. Experimental trials have been conducted using different surfaces with varied textures and slopes, resulting in successful climbs in most cases. However, certain surfaces proved too slippery for the bot to ascend.

Recent clinical trials combining colon cancer treatments with immune system activation have yielded significant benefits, prompting researchers to apply customized treatment approaches based on individual patient data. This involves determining the optimal timing and dosage of treatments that maximize their compatibility with the patient's immune system reaction. To this end, a novel technique is proposed that integrates patient-specific colon cancer and immune system models to forecast the effect of distinct treatment combinations. To identify the most effective treatments, the model simulates various treatment schedules, assessing their efficacy and stability. This study utilizes the Fokker-Planck equation to analyze the probability distribution of the immune system's colonization state over time, with the objective of optimizing treatments for clinical trials. The results validate the model's capability to customize treatments and predict their outcomes, offering a valuable tool for clinical application.

Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication holds significant importance, particularly in crowded areas, where unwanted interference from nearby transmissions can cause significant data loss. A novel approach is presented, which uses deep learning to develop an automatic scheduling system that relies on real-time data and doesn't need manual human input. By leveraging a large dataset of real-world video traffic, a deep network is trained to predict the data transfer rates of nearby devices based on the transfer data of a target device. This predicted information is then used to optimize transmission parameters, such as power and frequency, to minimize data loss and ensure seamless communication. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through comprehensive simulations and comparative analyses with other conventional scheduling methods. The results show that this proposed method delivers substantial improvements in overall data quality and reduce data transfer errors by up to 80% and 88% respectively, with the added benefits of reduced complex human intervention and faster system response times.

This research proves that helicity is preserved in the compressible Euler equations for smooth solutions with any spatial and temporal regularity. Moreover, it demonstrates the local $C^\infty$ well-posedness of the helical smoothing operator, a tool employed to establish conservation of helicity. The development of sophisticated frequency splitting and frequency localization techniques plays a key role in this proof.

For the Davey-Stewartson II equations, we find that the reflection coefficient has an absolute value of more than one in specific situations, which happens when certain conditions are met regarding wind direction and depth. The background three-dimensional flow meets certain criteria, and as a result, so does the two-dimensional perturbation. The circumstances in which this occurs involve an infinite number of interactions between waves and the mean flow. The conditions required can be realized through various methods, including altering wind patterns and water depth. The resulting behavior of the reflection coefficient is dependent on the signs of certain key components. The presence of multiple modes in the perturbation affects how the reflection coefficient behaves for different modes. The occurrence of a large reflection coefficient is tied to the presence of perturbation modes that interact in a particular way with the mean flow. The characteristics of these modes determine whether a large reflection coefficient will be observed, and if so, what its value will be. The background mean flow's properties are crucial in determining which perturbation modes will be active and thus influence the reflection coefficient's behavior. The properties of the background mean flow also determine the properties of the perturbation modes, and thus play a key role in determining the reflection coefficient's significant behavior.

Calculations involving the remaining eccentricity of merging binary black holes' inspirals are carried out using post-Newtonian theory for masses greater than 5 solar masses with eccentricities up to 0.99. A matched-filtering analysis based on the LIGO's 2015 design is applied to determine the detectability of gravitational waves, and the effects of neglecting higher-order eccentricity terms and the reliance on lower-order terms are examined. It's found that for masses above 20 solar masses with eccentricities of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.9, the relative error in predicting eccentricity at detection threshold is 3%, 10%, and 30%, respectively. A useful approximation for predicting eccentricity at the detection threshold without needing higher-order terms is also provided.

A proposed enhancer design, powered by a free-electron laser oscillator, would significantly increase the intensity of X-rays through a combination of gain switching and nonlinear effects at the expense of spectral broadening. This recursive process of amplification would be driven by an interplay between the oscillator's harmonic frequencies and the intrinsic damping of the enhancer. As short-wavelength X-rays are generated, they would trigger gain switching, leading to a rapid increase in density and further enhancement of the X-ray flux. This innovative system would enable researchers to study extremely high-density, short-wavelength states that were previously inaccessible.

In the context of incident recognition in dynamic networks, our research focuses on designing an effective model that can identify anomalies in real-time online interactions among social media users. By employing dynamic network analysis and combining structural features with temporal characteristics, our model addresses the challenges of online incident reporting, false information dissemination, and real-time tracking of incidents. By analyzing user relationships and node attributes, our model extracts relevant structural and attribute features from the incident network, followed by extraction of temporal characteristics through time-series analysis of incident edges and nodes. Our novel features, including spatial replication, structural cohesion, and temporal continuity, complement well-established metrics such as degree, closeness, and autocorrelation to enhance performance. Our results demonstrate the accuracy of our approach using synthetic datasets generated from models like preferential attachment and independent branching, as well as real-world datasets from Chinese social media platforms, specifically instances of "jaj Jared" which typically signify online incidents.

Researchers find that in a medium with varying density, the developing discontinuity travels faster than in a uniform medium, reaching approximately twice the speed of sound, regardless of whether the initial pressure or density differs. To resolve this, models must account for factors such as energy fluctuations or pressure and density gradients. Introducing small fluctuations into the medium's density leads to the creation of unusual solutions involving sound waves, shocks, and rarefactions. These unusual solutions don't match physical expectations, highlighting the need for a mechanism to select preferred solutions. By considering entropy changes, a preferred solution emerges, aligning with physical expectations. This mechanism addresses an longstanding issue in astrophysics and fluid dynamics known as the collapsing shock problem.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. This necessity not only hampers the user experience but also hampers business operations if the explanations are insufficient. The main objective of this paper is to investigate how the requirements engineering field can contribute to addressing this challenge. A comprehensive study involving extensive interviews with prominent researchers in the machine learning and explainable AI fields has been conducted. Based on this study, a framework for incorporating requirements engineering concepts into the explainable AI research domain has been developed. This framework's initial outcomes are presented in the form of lessons learned. A conceptual model that facilitates the alignment of user needs with relevant research sub-domains has been proposed. This model is expected to facilitate further inquiry into this area.

From human samples, histopathological examination provides critical insights into disease diagnosis and treatment by uncovering biological processes. Deep learning, now widely applied in histopathology, has shown significant potential in improving colorectal polyps diagnosis and adenoma development assessment. Previous research relied on publicly available datasets, such as the UniToPatho dataset, which comprises its original counterpart named UniTo. Originally containing 214 images, the dataset has been expanded to 1242 images, encompassing stained and digitized sections of 121 colorectal polyps from 47 patients. Each polyp was manually annotated to identify viable tissue, luminal areas, and carmine-red stained nuclei, providing an rich platform for research in machine learning and histopathology.

The structure of the dataset is illustrated in Figure 1. Each image from the dataset includes three regions: the mucosa, the lumen, and the cytoplasm. The cytoplasm section, specifically, contains carmine-red stained nuclei. These regions are employed to train models for tissue viability assessment and event detection within the areas.

In a situation where a source encoder attempts to eliminate transmission errors, there may still be unintended data leaks occurring outside of standard decoding errors. We investigate the theoretical bounds of these data leaks from a information-theory standpoint. Our analysis reveals that data leaks can be comprehended through a linear perspective and that the leaks' zero-miss rate counterpart offers insights into the encoded data's coverage. Furthermore, we demonstrate that data leaks can be represented by a graph, where the rate of leaks corresponds to the size of specific clique families within that graph. This graphical framework enables the computation of the leaks' rate and tolerance via coefficient matrices and polynomial functions respectively. We also establish connections between the leaks' critical rate, tolerance, and combinatorial problems like the integer programming and the partitions with equal sums. Lastly, we present a study on the general source encoding with data leaks, which may be applicable to a variety of real-world data encoding scenarios.

Remote sensing image quality, particularly for Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), largely depends on the performance of its imaging system and signal processing techniques. High-resolution images are crucial in various applications such as crop monitoring, flood risk assessment, and urban planning. Unfortunately, conventional SAR imaging involves trade-offs between resolution and range due to limited bandwidth and antenna size. This research presents a novel deep learning approach, MrSARP, which utilizes radar wave physics to develop a generative model for SAR image enhancement. Built upon the SAR imaging process, MrSARP, combines signal scattering and propagation, to create a realistic training dataset for its network. This generative model can learn and incorporate image physics from lower to higher frequency components, producing better results than existing methods while maintaining network simplicity. Our experiments using real-airborne SAR images demonstrate the efficacy of MrSARP in improving resolution without affecting range performance.

A new optimization method is proposed, combining Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variations with Bayesian maximization, to enhance its efficiency and accuracy. The approach involves a two-stage process: first, Bayesian maximization identifies the optimal quantum circuit parameters within a predefined search space; second, these parameters are utilized to construct a enhanced QAOA algorithm. The method overcomes a common QAOA limitation by facilitating the search for optimal parameters without necessitating their eventual use, thus enabling a more comprehensive exploration of the parameter space. The proposed method exhibits improved performance in specific contexts, such as solving MaxCut problems on a particular circuit circuit.

This research proposes a precise method for identifying areas where two or more ellipses intersect. The proposed algorithm calculates the intersection regions between multiple ellipses in a systematic way, without relying on case-specific techniques or approximations that may lead to partial results. The algorithm can efficiently compute the complete intersection region between two ellipses in a time complexity of O(k), where k represents the number of intersections. This method has been verified to produce correct results for all possible cases and can be applied dynamically to determine the intersection regions between moving ellipses. The algorithm provides a means to determine whether an ellipse intersects a circle, a segment, or a rectangle, allowing its utilization in more complex applications such as game development and computer graphics.

A fundamental concept in order theory, q-discovery reflects a measure of how closely tied two orders are. It has been explored in the past with regards to linearly ordered sets, but this research aims to extend its application to areas with continuous duration. Building on previous work regarding q discovery with respect to intervals, this thesis seeks to provide a more comprehensive set of definitions that also considers the presence of "durational holes". These definitions will be compared to the corresponding literature on q discovery with linear orders, and their relationship to other theoretical frameworks, such as q discovery with weighted orders and the concept of correspondences, will also be examined. Furthermore, this thesis identifies specific definitions of q discovery that are relevant to the study of ritual durations.

A self-consistent mean-field calculation along with a Gutzwiller ansatz is performed for the extended Hubbard model on a triangular lattice with both spin and orbital symmetry breaking parameters. The mean-field calculation reveals a complex phase diagram with different types of magnetic orders. However, a more accurate treatment using the Gutzwiller ansatz shows that several of these magnetic orders collapse at zero temperature due to the effect of quantum fluctuations. In contrast, other orders remain stable under increased temperature. By analyzing the behavior of quantum fluctuations, it becomes evident that the mechanism behind the loss of these magnetic orders is a phenomenon known as order-by-disorder. Furthermore, the Gutzwiller ansatz treatment also provides insights into the behavior of chemical potential oscillations, which are utilized as an indicator of heavy fermion behavior. The result shows that these oscillations are present in certain parts of the phase diagram, confirming that the model describes a heavy-fermion system.

Vertebral localization and recognition are crucial for spinal surgery planning, but the process is labor-intensive and time-consuming due to the complex and deformed spinal system. Previous studies have largely relied on primitive point-based methods, which are prone to errors and inconsistencies. This research introduces an advanced vertebral localization and recognition system that utilizes a coordinated approach of spine alignment and anatomically constrained optimization to quickly and accurately identify vertebral bodies. By initially correcting spinal deformation and establishing corresponding point-to-plate correspondence, the vertebral centroids can be accurately calculated. Subsequently, an anatomically constrained 6-degree of freedom optimization is employed to derive vertebral axes and orientations. The proposed system has been validated and evaluated using 188 full-spine CT scans, which demonstrated high accuracy and robustness for vertebral localization and recognition, especially in side and apex views. The research provides a highly reliable and efficient solution for automatically locating and recognizing vertebral bodies across a wide range of cases. The developed method has been successfully used in clinical settings and shown to produce results on par with experienced radiologists. The research provides a comprehensive framework for developing advanced spinal surgery planning tools. The developed software is now available for public use via a GitHub repository. The research has been publicly disclosed with the IEEE copyright holder.

A CFT's C-crosscap universality class is analyzed from the perspective of random thermodynamics by considering the asymptotic behavior of the 2D Ising model's partition function, which can be expressed in terms of the Gaussian free field's Green's function. This involves manipulating loop correlators with various weights and orientations, which are explored in detail. Our investigation demonstrates that gauge invariance dictates the form of the leading asymptotic term of the partition function, which occurs when the crosscap's Euler characteristic is -1. This result also holds for other CFTs, including the free fermion models Fermonic and C*fermonic, as well as the chirality models ChIsing and CIsing, which allows us to confirm a previously proposed conjecture. Our work further establishes the relationship between the loop correlators' asymptotic behavior and the structural constants of the quiver representation. Moreover, the integration over the gauge field's periodic component in the measure's normalization is shown to produce the Asymptotic Gaussian Free Field, which represents the universal component of the C-crosscap universality class. Our investigation reveals that the asymptotic behavior of the partition function is characterized by a power law, with the exponent depending on the structural characteristics of the quiver representation.

Given a projective variety of dimension d, a and b are morphism-free pairs of projects, each leading to the same variety under dimension and embedding transformations. We combine their respective smooth d-dimensional bundles with trivial fibers, applying the relative quantum topology to the paired structures. This results in a d-dimensional relative Euler characteristic, ε, and a d-dimensional relative signature, σ, which remain invariant across a, b. When the variety is a d-dimensional projective line, this theorem aligns with established results, extending existing principles to higher dimensional scenarios. We utilize our findings to demonstrate a relationship between the structure of the singularity's receptor and the structure of the variety's smooth model, revealing new connections between the topology of the variety and the representation of the fundamental group to the variety's singular locus. We also identify key obstructions in the relative quantum topology, establishing a significant extension to existing theorems. These discoveries enable a comprehensive understanding and precise calculation of the relative Euler characteristic and signature across a wide range of varieties. We also demonstrate the unwrapping theorem for the relative quantum topology, a critical tool in the field. These breakthroughs were facilitated by the creation of a new quantum algebra, Q(z), which we introduce.

Two piezoelectric materials, cut at the 36-degree crystallographic angle, are placed near each other, resulting in an acoustic gap that narrows and eventually becomes zero, enabling unprecedentedly strong transmission of sound waves. This phenomenon, driven by the resonance of the materials, occurs regardless of the direction in which the crystals are aligned. Our theoretical and experimental findings reveal that, due to the resonance, the usual attenuation of sound waves by the materials disappears, and a remarkable increase in transmission up to 100% is achieved.

We introduce a cutting-edge method for optically manipulating polariton aggregates at a microsecond scale, surpassing previous techniques which operated at millisecond speeds. By incorporating optical confinement and precise control of excitation, we can rapidly switch aggregate state transitions. This advancement opens doors for novel applications such as ultra-fast light sources, neurocomputer interfaces, and photonic switch systems.

The exoplanet K2-22 b, a super-Earth that orbits a low-active star with a relatively short 3.35-day period, has been found to exhibit unique behavior. Observations of this planet have revealed the presence of a mysterious deep depression in its optical light curve, accompanied by the emergence of a bright giant storm that appears to transitory changes in the planet's atmospheric properties. Recent studies using the Kepler space telescope revealed the detection of a small-scale atmospheric phenomenon known as a "small-scale storm or wave," albeit without evidence of its lower atmospheric processes. A more recent analysis employing the Large Binocular Telescope Observer (LBT) proved to be successful in capturing a full transit of the planet, providing a broader understanding of its lower atmosphere by revealing key features. 

In particular, the LBT data revealed the presence of heavy grain sediments in the planet's lower atmosphere, which are thought to be the result of increased wind velocities in this region, contrary to initial predictions of slower speeds. Additionally, the LBT observations indicate a significant increase in mass loss in the planet's lower atmosphere, suggesting that any additional wind energy generated by internal heat or other factors would likely boost this process. 

A more detailed examination of the LBT data using various models confirmed that the deep atmosphere is characterized by high levels of grain content, elevated temperatures, and increased atmospheric pressure, all of which are consistent with the observed transmission spectra.

We establish a condition, based on the coherence of the Milnor algebra, that implies the coherence of the Milnor algebra of a seminormal ring. This condition is met when the critical set of a graded ring is a flat subspace. This coincidence of coherence and flatness of the critical set is the key to our proof that the Milnor fiber coherence of a reduced isolated critical point is equivalent to the projective space coherence of its embedding. This result extends known findings for space and hypersurface singularities.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Designed for.NET environments, this tool facilitates data preparation, feature engineering, and other data transformation operations. Developed atop.NET Standard 2.1 and compatible with.NET Core 3.0+, Daany consists of multiple VS projects that can be easily installed as a NuGet package. At its core, Daany utilizes the DataFrame data structure, complemented by data science and linear algebra capabilities, including time series decomposition (SSA, STL, ARIMA) and optimization methods (SGD). The library also integrates matrix and vector operations, as well as data plotting functionality. Daany's implementation bears similarities to Python's Pandas library. This guide serves as a comprehensive developer manual, outlining Daany's features, functionality, and usage, as well as a roadmap for its future development.

The argument that mathematics serves as the superior tool for the natural scientist to utilize was a perspective argued by Augustus de Morgan in the 19th century, and this viewpoint has been supported by prominent mathematicians throughout history, including Galileo. This essay seeks to demonstrate that Galileo's mathematical approach was ultimately the key factor contributing to his failure to integrate philosophy into his own scientific endeavors, and as a result, he missed an opportunity to develop a comprehensive philosophical framework for his scientific work.

New perspectives on Saha's ionization are offered through non-Gaussian analytical and numerical modeling, which contrasts with conventional Gaussian theories. By reevaluating Saha's equation, it becomes evident that under primitive conditions, the number of electrons interacts in a manner that exhibits decreasing variability as temperatures rise, ultimately resulting in the cessation of electron-proton fusion at a specific temperature. This stopping temperature is found to be around 0.7 MeV, indicating that even at the elevated temperature of the Cosmic Dark Age (~0.24 eV), electron captures had already ceased, with far-reaching implications for the pre-CMB universe.

This study employs the magnetohydrodynamics equations, integrated into a simulation framework that includes a fully adapted Particle-In-Cell model, to analyze magnetic island merging. Utilizing the OKEANES code, we have accurately calculated the complex interactions between magnetic field stresses and particle currents. Our findings demonstrate that ion motion responds in real-time to changing electric and magnetic fields, while electron behavior is influenced by both electric and magnetic forces, as well as electrostatic forces, depending on the location of the PIC cell. Our analysis includes a thorough examination of the dynamics of magnetic island merging using the VMEC code's equilibrium configuration of the National Spherical Toroidal Vacuum Facility. Our results reveal that any variation in magnetic field stress and particle flow corresponds to distinct changes in local electric and magnetic fields, housing charged particles. Furthermore, we have identified that when one island leads another in velocity, a rotating current begins to form within the overlap zone, eventually breaking down into smaller structures once certain thresholds are met. Our study also confirms that any current detected in the vicinity of the fusion edge must be closely aligned with the local magnetic field, as any perpendicular orientation would signify an electric field, opposing our assumptions of quasineutral conditions.

Scribe is an innovative system that allows a main program to delegate tasks to subprograms, known as scribes, which can share the main program's resources. While a scribe subprogram runs within the main program's memory space, it operates independently, receiving allocated tasks from the main program. If a scribe subprogram executes a task, the main program is notified of the scribe ID, task identifier, and execution results. In the event of a scribe subprogram malfunction, the main program can initiate a task restart or terminate the malfunctioning scribe, preventing performance degradation of the main program.
